title: Observation of complete delocalization in disordered photonic lattices
comment: Main Text (5 pages, 4 figures); Supplemental Material (11 pages, 10 figures); Supplemental Material is added as an Ancillary file; Comments are welcome
summary: We present the exceptional phenomenon of complete absence of Anderson localization, and perfect transmission of particles, in a completely disordered diamond-dot chain. We analytically show a proof for the condition to observe this exceptional phenomenon, based on a transparent window emerging from a geometrical condition. We support our theoretical prediction by numerical simulations and direct experimental observation of the transmission probabilities of the light in a femtosecond laser-written diamond-dot photonic lattices. We additionally show that for a $π$ effective magnetic flux, extreme localization of the light in the same system may occur, independently on the specific geometry. Our results open up an excellent platform for controlling the transmission of energy from ballistic to zero transmission, in a completely disordered lattice system..

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that Anderson localization can be completely suppressed in a fully disordered diamond-dot chain under a specific geometrical condition, allowing perfect particle transmission. It provides analytical proof, numerical simulations, and experimental verification using femtosecond laser-written photonic lattices. Additionally, with a π effective magnetic flux, extreme localization occurs regardless of geometry, offering a platform to control energy transmission from ballistic to zero.
AI.motivation: To investigate the exceptional phenomenon where Anderson localization is completely absent in a fully disordered system, and to demonstrate controllable transmission from ballistic to zero transmission.
AI.method: Analytical proof of the condition for absence of Anderson localization based on a geometrical transparent window; numerical simulations; direct experimental observation using femtosecond laser-written diamond-dot photonic lattices.
AI.result: Complete absence of Anderson localization and perfect transmission in a disordered diamond-dot chain under a specific geometrical condition; extreme localization with π effective magnetic flux independent of geometry.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a platform for controlling energy transmission from ballistic to zero in completely disordered lattice systems.

title: Truncated Wigner dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses
summary: Quantum spin glasses are often considered testbeds for studying quantum optimization algorithms and as such have been the subject of various quantum advantage claims. Here we investigate the near adiabatic dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses within the (discrete) truncated Wigner approximation (TWA). Benchmarks on small systems show that TWA recovers sample-to-sample fluctuations of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter, over a wide range of annealing times, with increasing fidelity when the system size increases. We extract critical exponents from the Binder cumulant in line with theoretical expectations, reproducing recent quantum experiments. The computational cost of the method is minimal and it can easily be applied to tens of thousands of qubits.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates near-adiabatic dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses using the discrete truncated Wigner approximation (TWA), showing that TWA accurately recovers sample-to-sample fluctuations of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter and critical exponents from the Binder cumulant, with minimal computational cost scalable to tens of thousands of qubits.
AI.motivation: Quantum spin glasses are testbeds for studying quantum optimization algorithms and have been subject to various quantum advantage claims; the authors aim to investigate their near-adiabatic dynamics with an efficient computational method.
AI.method: The authors use the discrete truncated Wigner approximation (TWA) to study near-adiabatic dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses, benchmarking on small systems and comparing against Edwards-Anderson order parameter fluctuations and Binder cumulant critical exponents.
AI.result: TWA recovers sample-to-sample fluctuations of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter with increasing fidelity as system size increases, over a wide range of annealing times. Critical exponents extracted from the Binder cumulant match theoretical expectations and reproduce recent quantum experiments. The method has minimal computational cost and can handle tens of thousands of qubits.
AI.conclusion: TWA is an efficient and accurate method for studying large-scale quantum spin glass dynamics, capable of reproducing experimental results while being scalable to tens of thousands of qubits, with minimal computational overhead.

title: Solving Nonequilibrium Dynamics via Influence Matrix Bootstrap: Floquet-PXP Model
summary: Studies of integrable systems have profoundly deepened the fundamental understanding of quantum many-body physics. While equilibrium properties such as ground states and thermodynamics can often be characterized efficiently, accurately characterizing nonequilibrium integrable dynamics remains a significant challenge. Here, we address this problem in the "Rule 201" quantum cellular automaton, an integrable Trotterization of the PXP Hamiltonian. Using the tensor-network approach of the influence matrix, we develop local conditions called generalized zipper conditions that allow exact solutions of local dynamics. We also introduce a numerical bootstrap method for solving influence matrices with finite but relatively large bond dimensions. This uncovers a rich landscape of nonequilibrium behavior exhibiting initial-state dependence. As an example, we investigate the fate of persistent oscillating dynamics under local non-integrable perturbations, and present analytical results for non-thermal relaxation constrained by conservation laws. We also obtain numerically exact results for entanglement growth across a broad class of initial states. Furthermore, from an information-theoretic perspective, we identify a refined structure of multitime correlations termed the hidden Markov order: the memory encoded in the dynamics separates into finite-length and long-range distributed components, which becomes transparent in an exact split-index matrix-product-state representation of the influence matrix. Our approach enables unified investigations of nonthermalizing and thermalizing regimes of nonequilibrium dynamics within a single analytically tractable model, and can be tested experimentally in state-of-the-art quantum simulators such as Rydberg atom arrays.

AI.tldr: The paper develops exact and numerical methods (generalized zipper conditions and bootstrap) for solving local dynamics in the integrable "Rule 201" quantum cellular automaton, uncovering initial-state-dependent nonequilibrium behavior, non-thermal relaxation under perturbations, and hidden Markov order in multitime correlations, with experimental relevance to Rydberg atom arrays.
AI.motivation: Accurately characterizing nonequilibrium integrable dynamics remains a significant challenge, even though equilibrium properties like ground states and thermodynamics are often efficiently described.
AI.method: Using the tensor-network influence matrix approach, the authors develop generalized zipper conditions for exact local dynamics and a numerical bootstrap method for influence matrices with finite bond dimensions. They also employ a split-index matrix-product-state representation to reveal hidden Markov order.
AI.result: They uncover initial-state-dependent nonequilibrium behavior, provide analytical results for non-thermal relaxation under local non-integrable perturbations, obtain numerically exact entanglement growth for various initial states, and identify a hidden Markov order structure where memory separates into finite-length and long-range distributed components.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables unified study of nonthermalizing and thermalizing regimes within a single tractable model and is testable in Rydberg atom array quantum simulators.

title: Indefinite Quantum Causality
comment: 76 pages + a 2-pages Appendix; 32 figures + 1 in the Appendix
summary: In recent years, operational approaches to quantum foundations have been developed as a means of understanding the core principles and distinctive features of quantum theory. Such approaches typically view physical processes as sequences of operations, with earlier operations serving as causes of later effects. However, a growing literature is emerging on the possibility of relaxing this assumption and allowing for quantum indefiniteness in the causal order. This development stems from a variety of motivations, both fundamental and applied, including exploring the role of causality in quantum theory, the interplay between quantum theory and general relativity, and higher-order quantum computing. A prominent offshoot of this development is the emergence of indefinite causal order as a feasible resource for quantum information processing. This review provides an overview of the current state of the art in the field, covering the methodology underlying indefinite quantum causality within the so-called "process matrix formalism", outlining key results and experimental implementations, and discussing recent advances.

AI.tldr: This review covers indefinite causal order in quantum theory, where causal structure is not fixed a priori, using the process matrix formalism, including key results, experiments, and recent advances, with applications from foundational causality studies to quantum information processing.
AI.motivation: To understand core principles of quantum theory by relaxing the assumption of fixed causal order, and to explore the interplay between quantum theory and general relativity, as well as higher-order quantum computing.
AI.method: Operational approach via the process matrix formalism, which allows for quantum indefiniteness in causal order without presupposing a fixed causal structure.
AI.result: Indefinite causal order has emerged as a feasible resource for quantum information processing, with several experimental implementations realized.
AI.conclusion: The field provides a promising avenue for understanding quantum theory's foundational causality aspects and offers practical advantages in quantum information tasks.

title: Efficient classical representation and quantum state preparation of complete active space wavefunctions
summary: Quantum computers promise to solve the electronic structure problem for a large class of molecules. However, the performance of relevant quantum algorithms hinges on preparing initial states with substantial overlap with the target eigenvector. For classically challenging molecules with strong electron correlation, starting from multi-reference states, such as complete active space (CAS) wavefunctions is necessary. Unfortunately, the most advanced state preparation protocols applied to such states result in a gate complexity that scales exponentially with the active space size $d$. In fact, even encoding a CAS state classically is traditionally believed to be intractable for chemically relevant systems. Here, we draw insights from the recently introduced Quantum Paldus Transform (QPT) to show that there exists an efficient classical representation of CAS states and to design a new state preparation routine outperforming previous ones. The QPT represents a transformation from the Fock basis to a friendlier symmetry-adapted basis. Our main contribution consists in showing that CAS states expanded in this basis can efficiently be represented as a matrix product state (MPS) with a bond dimension scaling as $O(d^2)$. One can then efficiently load the MPS on a quantum computer and use the inverse QPT to transform the state to the Fock basis. Moreover, our method can easily be extended to the efficient preparation of CAS states in first quantisation with similar complexity. Crucially, we demonstrate that the complexity of both state preparation protocols only grows polynomially as $O(d^3)$ , which constitutes to the best of our knowledge an exponential improvement over the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new method for efficiently preparing complete active space (CAS) states on quantum computers by leveraging the Quantum Paldus Transform (QPT). CAS states can be represented as matrix product states (MPS) with bond dimension O(d²), and state preparation complexity scales polynomially as O(d³), an exponential improvement over previous methods.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithms for solving the electronic structure problem require initial states with substantial overlap with target eigenvectors. For classically challenging molecules with strong electron correlation, multi-reference states like CAS wavefunctions are necessary, but existing state preparation protocols have gate complexity scaling exponentially with active space size d, and even classical encoding of CAS states is traditionally believed intractable.
AI.method: The authors use the Quantum Paldus Transform (QPT) to transform from the Fock basis to a symmetry-adapted basis. They show CAS states expanded in this basis can be efficiently represented as MPS with bond dimension O(d²). The MPS is loaded onto a quantum computer, and the inverse QPT transforms the state back to the Fock basis. The method extends to first quantisation with similar complexity.
AI.result: The complexity of both state preparation protocols grows polynomially as O(d³), which constitutes an exponential improvement over the state of the art. The bond dimension of the MPS representation scales as O(d²).
AI.conclusion: There exists an efficient classical representation of CAS states, and the new state preparation routine outperforms previous ones, enabling practical quantum advantage for classically challenging molecular systems with strong electron correlation.

title: Quantum deformations of $\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R}))$. Part I: Fidelity and experimental benchmarking
summary: This work explores the effects of both the standard quantum $q$-deformation and the non-standard $h$-deformation of the Hopf algebra $\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R}))$ on multi-qubit systems. By constructing the states of a Hilbert space of $N$ qubits through the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients associated with the deformed algebras, we show that these states naturally coincide with the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian of the $q$- and $h$-deformed Kittel-Shore models. We compare the resulting deformed states with those typically targeted in quantum information experiments, providing a bridge between algebraic constructions and experimentally relevant quantum resources. Fidelities with respect to the undeformed states are computed to establish how the quantum correlations are affected, both for few-qubit systems (including Dicke and non-Dicke states), and in the macroscopic limit ($N \to \infty$) through closed-form formulas derived for arbitrary Dicke states. The results reveal different behaviors between the two deformations. The $q$-deformation smoothly modifies the states and maintains a residual overlap with the original configurations, while the $h$-deformation rapidly makes the states orthogonal to their undeformed counterparts. Both models demand a standard $N^{-1}$ rescaling to preserve fidelity stability in the macroscopic limit.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how quantum $q$-deformation and non-standard $h$-deformation of the Hopf algebra $\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R}))$ affect multi-qubit systems. The deformed states correspond to eigenstates of deformed Kittel-Shore models. The $q$-deformation smoothly alters states with residual overlap, while $h$-deformation rapidly makes states orthogonal. Both require $N^{-1}$ rescaling to maintain fidelity stability in the macroscopic limit.
AI.motivation: To bridge algebraic constructions (deformed Hopf algebras) with experimentally relevant quantum resources, by understanding how quantum deformations affect multi-qubit states and their correlations.
AI.method: Constructs $N$-qubit Hilbert space states using Clebsch-Gordan coefficients from $q$- and $h$-deformed $\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R}))$, showing they coincide with eigenstates of deformed Kittel-Shore models. Fidelities are computed for few-qubit and macroscopic ($N\to\infty$) Dicke states.
AI.result: $q$-deformation smoothly modifies states preserving residual overlap; $h$-deformation rapidly orthogonalizes states. Both deformations require $N^{-1}$ rescaling for fidelity stability in the macroscopic limit. Closed-form formulas for arbitrary Dicke states are derived.
AI.conclusion: The two deformations exhibit fundamentally different behaviors affecting quantum correlations, with implications for understanding deformed symmetries in quantum information contexts.

title: Local controllability of heralded quantum linear optics
summary: Photonic linear optical networks provide a versatile platform for quantum information processing and quantum state engineering. However, the set of states that can be generated using passive linear optics alone is fundamentally constrained by bosonic symmetries. Heralding, based on conditional measurements on auxiliary modes, is a widely used technique to overcome these limitations and effectively enlarge the set of accessible states. Despite the widespread use of heralding, it is often unclear how specific ancillary resources impact the overall reachability of the target space. In this work, we investigate the local controllability of photonic states in linear optical networks by analyzing the rank of the Jacobian of the output state with respect to the underlying unitary circuit, which provides a quantitative measure of the dimension of the accessible tangent space at a given configuration. Our analysis ranges from passive linear optics to heralded linear optics, where auxiliary resources and conditional measurements are included. Within this framework, we quantify how different resources enlarge the locally accessible state space beyond that of passive linear optics and determine the resources required for the Jacobian rank to reach its maximal value, thereby achieving full local controllability. As maximal local rank is a necessary condition for global reachability, our framework offers a systematic tool to assess and compare the accessible state space of measurement-based photonic architectures, and to establish practical criteria for the resources needed in high-dimensional quantum state engineering.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes local controllability of photonic states in linear optical networks by examining the rank of the Jacobian of the output state relative to the underlying unitary circuit. It quantifies how heralding and auxiliary resources expand the accessible state space beyond passive linear optics, determining conditions for full local controllability.
AI.motivation: Heralding (conditional measurements on auxiliary modes) is widely used to overcome the limitations of passive linear optics in quantum state engineering, but it is often unclear how specific ancillary resources impact the reachability of target quantum states.
AI.method: The authors investigate local controllability by analyzing the rank of the Jacobian of the output state with respect to the underlying unitary circuit, providing a quantitative measure of the dimension of the accessible tangent space at a given configuration. The analysis spans passive linear optics to heralded linear optics with auxiliary resources and conditional measurements.
AI.result: The framework quantifies how different resources enlarge the locally accessible state space beyond passive linear optics and identifies the resources required for the Jacobian rank to reach its maximal value, achieving full local controllability.
AI.conclusion: Maximal local rank is a necessary condition for global reachability. The framework provides a systematic tool to assess and compare accessible state spaces of measurement-based photonic architectures and establishes practical criteria for resources needed in high-dimensional quantum state engineering.

title: Nearest-neighbour gates are all you need: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes on a planar grid
summary: High-performance quantum low-density parity-check codes promise substantial reductions in the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but most constructions require long-range connectivity or qubit shuttling, both of which are difficult to realise in superconducting architectures. Here we introduce a family of quantum low-density parity-check codes that, for the first time, combines planar open-boundary layouts, finite-size advantages over surface codes, and syndrome extraction using only nearest-neighbour gates on a square grid of qubits. The key idea is to generate check-data connectivity dynamically: nearest-neighbour iSWAP walks both define the stabiliser supports and implement their measurement, avoiding the need for a long-range hardware graph. The resulting circuits achieve optimal constant-depth stabiliser measurement, independent of code size, and naturally remove leakage from the system by exchanging the role of check and data qubits at each syndrome extraction round. We find finite-size instances such as a [[323,14,15]] code, whose code-efficiency ratio is nearly an order of magnitude larger than that of rotated surface-code patches. At around 30 circuit qubits per logical qubit, the best directional tile-code layouts reduce the per-logical per-round logical error rate by up to a factor of 1000 relative to rotated surface-code memories. These results show that the advantages of quantum low-density parity-check codes can survive compilation into strictly planar nearest-neighbour circuits, bringing low-overhead fault-tolerant memories closer to near-term hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a family of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes that combine planar open-boundary layouts, finite-size advantages over surface codes, and syndrome extraction using only nearest-neighbour gates on a square grid. Using dynamic check-data connectivity via nearest-neighbour iSWAP walks, the approach achieves constant-depth stabiliser measurement, natural leakage removal, and significant gains in logical error rate (up to 1000×) and code efficiency compared to rotated surface codes.
AI.motivation: High-performance quantum LDPC codes promise reduced overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but existing constructions require long-range connectivity or qubit shuttling, which are impractical in superconducting architectures. The authors aim to bridge this gap by designing codes compatible with planar, nearest-neighbour hardware.
AI.method: The key innovation is dynamic check-data connectivity: nearest-neighbour iSWAP walks define stabiliser supports and implement their measurement simultaneously, eliminating the need for a long-range hardware graph. This yields constant-depth stabiliser measurement circuits independent of code size, with leakage naturally removed by swapping check and data qubit roles each round.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate finite-size instances like a [[323,14,15]] code with nearly an order of magnitude larger code-efficiency ratio than rotated surface-code patches. At ~30 circuit qubits per logical qubit, the best directional tile-code layouts achieve up to 1000× reduction in per-logical per-round logical error rate compared to rotated surface-code memories.
AI.conclusion: The advantages of quantum LDPC codes can survive compilation into strictly planar nearest-neighbour circuits, bringing low-overhead fault-tolerant memories closer to near-term hardware implementations.

title: Optimal Ansatz-free Hamiltonian Learning In Situ
summary: Characterizing the features of a Hamiltonian that governs a quantum system serves as a fundamental subroutine of quantum device calibration, signal sensing, and error correction. Recent works proposed protocols have achieved the optimal Heisenberg-limited scaling learning ansatz-free Hamiltonians from their real-time evolutions without fully specifying interaction structures. However, these protocols rely on both deep circuits with interleaving probes and control, and extremely short time resolution, making them difficult to implement on near- and intermediate-term in situ quantum experiments. In this work, we propose a computationally efficient, control-free, and ancilla-free algorithm that uses only Pauli product state preparation and measurement, and learns an ansatz-free Hamiltonian $H$ with $||H||\leqΛ$ in total evolution time of $Θ(\fracΛ{ε^2}\log(\fracΛε))$. The evolution time cost of our algorithm is optimal for any control-free protocols as we further prove a lower bound of $Ω(\fracΛ{ε^2}\log(\fracΛε))$. Technically, our method introduces a randomized-sampling framework that combines band-limited kernel-based time sampling with a displacement sieve for Hamiltonian structure learning. The characteristic probe time resolution depends only on $Λ$ instead of $\varepsilon$, which makes our protocol especially appealing in the high-precision regime for sensing and calibration applications. We also show that the algorithm maintains the same asymptotic total evolution time in the presence of state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) noise when the Hamiltonian is local after calibration. Our results demonstrate the fundamental cost of experimentally friendly Hamiltonian learning and provide a practical route to rigorous in situ characterization of near-term quantum platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a computationally efficient, control-free, and ancilla-free algorithm for learning ansatz-free Hamiltonians from real-time evolutions, achieving Heisenberg-limited scaling with optimal total evolution time Θ(Λ/ε² log(Λ/ε)), using only Pauli product state preparation and measurement, while being practical for near-term quantum experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing Hamiltonian learning protocols achieving optimal Heisenberg-limited scaling require both deep circuits with interleaving probes and control, and extremely short time resolution, making them difficult to implement in near- and intermediate-term in situ quantum experiments. A more experimentally friendly approach is needed.
AI.method: The algorithm introduces a randomized-sampling framework that combines band-limited kernel-based time sampling with a displacement sieve for Hamiltonian structure learning. It uses only Pauli product state preparation and measurement, requires no control or ancilla qubits, and the characteristic probe time resolution depends only on Λ (the Hamiltonian norm bound) rather than ε (the precision).
AI.result: The algorithm achieves total evolution time of Θ(Λ/ε² log(Λ/ε)), which is proven optimal for any control-free protocols via a matching lower bound of Ω(Λ/ε² log(Λ/ε)). The algorithm maintains the same asymptotic total evolution time in the presence of SPAM noise when the Hamiltonian is local after calibration.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates the fundamental cost of experimentally friendly Hamiltonian learning and provides a practical route to rigorous in situ characterization of near-term quantum platforms, being especially appealing in the high-precision regime for sensing and calibration applications.

title: Entanglement Scaling and Problem Structure in Quantum Approximate and Adiabatic Optimization Algorithms
summary: Entanglement is widely regarded as a key resource underlying the power of quantum algorithms and their potential to achieve quantum advantage. With the emergence of variational quantum algorithms, however, questions have arisen regarding how entanglement relates to problem structure and algorithmic performance in near-term quantum applications. Here, we examine this relationship through the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), a specific class of variational algorithms, applied to the MaxCut problem. We show that suboptimal variational parameter training can significantly modify the observed entanglement profile, obscuring its scaling behavior. By employing a high-performance optimizer, we find empirical evidence that QAOA exhibits entanglement scaling consistent with that of fermionic Gaussian states (up to a scaling factor) across a broad range of MaxCut instances. We further compare these results with adiabatic quantum computation, observing annealing-schedule-dependent entanglement profiles whose scaling behavior differs markedly from that of QAOA. Together, these findings provide new insight into how entanglement manifests in and distinguishes these two algorithmic paradigms, highlighting its connection to both computational performance and application structure.

AI.tldr: This paper studies entanglement scaling in QAOA applied to MaxCut, finding that with proper optimization, QAOA exhibits entanglement scaling similar to fermionic Gaussian states, which differs from that of adiabatic quantum computation.
AI.motivation: To understand how entanglement relates to problem structure and algorithmic performance in variational quantum algorithms, particularly whether entanglement scaling patterns are intrinsic to QAOA or obscured by suboptimal training.
AI.method: Applied QAOA to MaxCut instances with high-performance optimizers to study entanglement scaling; compared results with adiabatic quantum computation under different annealing schedules.
AI.result: Suboptimal variational parameter training can obscure entanglement scaling behavior. With proper optimization, QAOA shows entanglement scaling consistent with fermionic Gaussian states across many MaxCut instances. Adiabatic quantum computation exhibits annealing-schedule-dependent entanglement profiles with markedly different scaling.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement scaling distinguishes QAOA from adiabatic quantum computation, providing insight into how entanglement connects to computational performance and algorithmic structure in these paradigms.

title: Exact Markovian Dissipation Requires Singular Energy Resources
summary: The Gorini--Kossakowski--Lindblad--Sudarshan (GKLS) equation describes irreversible quantum dynamical semigroups. We show that this description cannot be exact under physically regular energy conditions. We prove that the open-system survival probability under physically regular energy conditions has sublinear decay, whereas any dissipative GKLS semigroup has a linear short-time decay. Hence exact Markovian dissipation requires singular energy resources: an unbounded-below total Hamiltonian or infinite initial energy, and a divergent interaction-energy moment. Therefore, a dissipative time-independent GKLS equation should be regarded as an effective description rather than the exact reduced dynamics of a Hamiltonian dilation satisfying physically regular energy conditions.

AI.tldr: The GKLS equation (quantum Markovian master equation) cannot be an exact description of open quantum systems under physically regular energy conditions, because it predicts linear short-time decay while real systems with bounded-below Hamiltonians and finite energy exhibit sublinear decay. Thus, exact Markovian dissipation requires singular energy resources (unbounded-below Hamiltonian, infinite energy), making the GKLS equation only an effective, not exact, description.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the GKLS equation can be an exact reduced dynamics derived from a Hamiltonian dilation under physically realistic energy conditions, rather than merely an effective approximation.
AI.method: The authors compare the short-time decay behavior of open-system survival probabilities: they prove that under physically regular energy conditions (bounded-below total Hamiltonian, finite initial energy, finite interaction-energy moment), the survival probability decays sublinearly, whereas any dissipative GKLS semigroup exhibits linear short-time decay. This contradiction shows exact Markovian dissipation is impossible under regular energy conditions.
AI.result: Physically regular energy conditions force sublinear short-time decay, while GKLS semigroups require linear short-time decay. Therefore, exact Markovian dissipation demands singular energy resources (unbounded-below Hamiltonian, infinite initial energy, divergent interaction-energy moment).
AI.conclusion: The dissipative time-independent GKLS equation should be regarded as an effective description, not the exact reduced dynamics of a Hamiltonian dilation satisfying physically regular energy conditions.

title: Distinguishing quantum processes with bounded coherent memory
summary: Distinguishing multi-time quantum processes is a fundamental task underlying the diagnosis, benchmarking, and learning of temporally correlated quantum dynamics. The standard benchmark for distinguishing two processes is the strategy-norm distance, which optimizes over arbitrary adaptive probing strategies but can require large coherent memory and time-dependent control. We introduce machines for autonomous distinction~($\mathsf{MAD}$s): probing strategies that apply the same quantum instrument at each time step, retain the full classical outcome record, and carry a coherent memory of dimension $d_A$. Optimizing over these strategies defines a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure, $d^{(N)}_{\mathsf{MAD}}(\mathbf{P}^N,\mathbf{Q}^N;d_A)$. We show that the resulting hierarchy is monotone in coherent memory and complete at finite times. Specifically, any admissible $N$-step probing strategy can be compiled into a single $\mathsf{MAD}$ with an internal counter and sufficiently large coherent memory, so the hierarchy saturates the strategy-norm benchmark. For recurrent processes generated by repeated system--environment interactions, we derive a single-step description that separates the generation of new distinguishing information from the propagation and decay of information generated at earlier times. Numerical results in a repeated-interaction model show that increasing coherent memory systematically improves the $\mathsf{MAD}$ success probability and closes the gap to the strategy-norm distance while remaining substantially more tractable to evaluate. $\mathsf{MAD}$ distinguishability therefore provides an operational and scalable framework for quantifying what can be learned about genuinely multi-time quantum processes with bounded coherent memory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Machines for Autonomous Distinction (MADs)—probing strategies using a fixed quantum instrument per time step, classical records, and bounded coherent memory—to define a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure for multi-time quantum processes. This hierarchy is monotone in memory, saturates the strategy-norm benchmark with sufficient memory, and provides a tractable framework for quantifying learnability of temporally correlated quantum dynamics.
AI.motivation: The standard strategy-norm distance for distinguishing multi-time quantum processes requires large coherent memory and time-dependent control, making it practically challenging. The authors aim to introduce a more operational and scalable distinguishability measure that accounts for bounded coherent memory resources.
AI.method: The authors define Machines for Autonomous Distinction (MADs), which apply the same quantum instrument at each time step, retain classical outcomes, and use a coherent memory of dimension d_A. They prove the hierarchy is monotone in memory, complete at finite times (any N-step strategy compiles into a MAD with a counter and sufficient memory), and derive a single-step description for recurrent processes.
AI.result: The hierarchy saturates the strategy-norm benchmark with sufficiently large coherent memory. Numerical results in a repeated-interaction model show systematic improvement in success probability with increasing coherent memory, closing the gap to the strategy-norm distance while remaining more tractable.
AI.conclusion: MAD distinguishability provides an operational and scalable framework for quantifying what can be learned about genuinely multi-time quantum processes under bounded coherent memory constraints.

title: Complexity of detecting large coefficients in the Pauli basis
summary: We study the problem of deciding, given a mechanism to prepare a quantum state $ρ$ and a value $\varepsilon > 0$, whether there is some non-identity Pauli matrix $P$ such that $|Tr(P ρ)| \geq \varepsilon$. We consider that the state $ρ$ is described as the result of tracing out some of the qubits of a pure state prepared by a circuit $C$, and we assume the promise that either there is a Pauli matrix satisfying the stated condition or, instead, that for all non-identity Pauli matrices $P$ it is the case that $|Tr(Pρ)|\leq \varepsilon/2$. The problem is in $QCMA$, and we prove that if it belongs to $BQP$ then $NP \subseteq BQP$. The result is obtained through a reduction from the minimum-weight code problem, and it holds even when $ρ$ is assumed to be a pure state (i.e. when no qubits are discarded) and $\varepsilon$ is constant. This resolves an open question regarding the existence of efficient tomographic procedures to find the largest coefficients of a quantum state in the Pauli basis: namely, they do not exist under the standard hypothesis $NP \nsubseteq BQP$.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that deciding whether a quantum state ρ has a significant Pauli coefficient (≥ε) is QCMA-complete, and if it were in BQP, then NP ⊆ BQP, implying efficient Pauli tomography does not exist under NP ⊄ BQP.
AI.motivation: To resolve whether efficient tomographic procedures exist for finding the largest coefficients of a quantum state in the Pauli basis.
AI.method: Reduction from the minimum-weight code problem to the Pauli coefficient decision problem, assuming the promise that either ∃P with |Tr(Pρ)|≥ε or ∀ non-identity P, |Tr(Pρ)|≤ε/2.
AI.result: The problem is in QCMA, and if it is also in BQP then NP ⊆ BQP. This holds even for pure states and constant ε.
AI.conclusion: Efficient Pauli tomography for finding large coefficients does not exist under the standard complexity assumption NP ⊄ BQP.

title: Passive-User Bell-State Loop-Back Key Establishment without Quantum Detectors at the User Nodes
summary: We propose and analyze a Bell-state extension of the Loop-Back quantum key distribution architecture for secret-key establishment between two passive users that do not require quantum transmitters or quantum detectors. In the proposed setting, a single active station, Alice, provides the entangled-state infrastructure, retains one qubit of an initially prepared Bell pair, and sends the traveling subsystem through two passive users, denoted by $B_1$ and $B_2$. Each passive user applies a local Pauli operation to the same traveling subsystem, so that the operation observed by Alice is only the effective composition $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=U_2U_1$. After the subsystem returns, Alice performs a Bell-state measurement and, using her private knowledge of the initial Bell state, deterministically identifies the effective Pauli operation. However, the individual factors $U_1$ and $U_2$ remain algebraically hidden from Alice whenever the local choices are uniformly and independently selected. The public effective operation acts as a parity-like constraint: each passive user can infer the operation applied by the other from its own private choice, while the active station learns only the global composition. This construction transfers the essential distributed-transformation mechanism of passive-user Loop-Back QKD to the entangled-state regime. Unlike single-qubit passive-user schemes, whose useful events are intrinsically post-selected, the Bell-state version is limited primarily by the success probability of the Bell-state measurement. We discuss the algebraic structure of the protocol, its interpretation as an infrastructure-assisted mediated key-establishment mechanism, and the physical assumptions required to protect passive Pauli modulators against active injection or Trojan-horse-type attacks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Bell-state extension of Loop-Back QKD where two passive users (B1, B2) without quantum transmitters/detectors share a traveling qubit from Alice's Bell pair, apply local Pauli operations, and establish a secret key through Alice's Bell-state measurement, with the protocol limited mainly by BSM success probability rather than post-selection.
AI.motivation: To extend passive-user Loop-Back QKD to the entangled-state regime, enabling two passive users (without quantum transmitters or detectors) to establish a secret key with the help of a single active station, while improving upon single-qubit passive-user schemes that suffer from post-selection inefficiencies.
AI.method: The active station Alice prepares a Bell pair, retains one qubit, and sends the other through two passive users B1 and B2 sequentially. Each user applies a local Pauli operation (Ui) to the traveling qubit. Alice performs a Bell-state measurement on the returned qubit and her retained qubit to identify the effective composition U_eff = U2U1. Since individual choices are uniformly independent, each user can infer the other's operation from their own private choice and the public U_eff, while Alice only learns the global composition.
AI.result: The Bell-state extension transfers the distributed-transformation mechanism of passive-user Loop-Back QKD to the entangled-state regime. Unlike single-qubit passive-user schemes requiring post-selection, the main limitation is the success probability of the Bell-state measurement. The protocol provides a parity-like constraint for key establishment between passive users.
AI.conclusion: The Bell-state Loop-Back QKD offers an infrastructure-assisted mediated key-establishment mechanism for passive users, with discussion of the algebraic structure and physical assumptions needed to protect passive Pauli modulators against active injection or Trojan-horse attacks.

title: Electrical Noise Produced by Micron-Sized Particles above a Surface Paul Trap
summary: Electric field noise produced by the surface of ion trap electrodes reduces the fidelity of quantum computing operations. Despite decades of investigation its microscopic origins remain unclear. Here, we measure electric field noise at trapping locations along the symmetry axis of a linear surface Paul trap. We find that noise levels vary by three orders-of-magnitude in one 600$\,μ$m section of the trap. Optical and scanning electron microscope images show micron-sized particles close to the trapping locations with the highest noise levels. We find that modeling the particles as a lossy dielectric with a effective loss tangent $\tanθ=0.33(0.06)$ describes the magnitude of the noise, as well as its spatial and frequency dependence. Our observations may explain the large variation of reported noise levels in literature.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies micron-sized particles on ion trap electrode surfaces as a dominant source of electric field noise, with noise levels varying by three orders of magnitude across a 600 μm section of a linear surface Paul trap, and models these particles as lossy dielectrics with an effective loss tangent of 0.33(0.06).
AI.motivation: Electric field noise from ion trap electrode surfaces degrades quantum computing fidelity, but its microscopic origins have remained unclear despite decades of investigation.
AI.method: The authors measured electric field noise at multiple trapping locations along the symmetry axis of a linear surface Paul trap, correlated noise levels with optical and scanning electron microscope imaging of surface contaminants, and modeled the particles as lossy dielectrics.
AI.result: Noise levels varied by three orders of magnitude within a 600 μm section; micron-sized particles were found near high-noise trapping locations; a lossy dielectric model with effective loss tangent tanθ = 0.33(0.06) accurately described the noise magnitude, spatial dependence, and frequency dependence.
AI.conclusion: Surface contaminant particles are a likely microscopic source of electric field noise, explaining the large variation in reported noise levels across different experiments.

title: Emergency hub placement with a neutral-atom quantum computer
summary: We study the problem of emergency operation center placement in disaster response, where a minimal number of hubs must be selected to ensure timely coverage of all affected locations. This task can be formulated as a minimum dominating set problem on a graph encoding reachability within a target response time. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical approximation framework that leverages neutral-atom quantum computers as independent set samplers. Candidate dominating sets are constructed from both small maximal independent sets and complements of large independent sets, and are subsequently refined via a lightweight classical procedure. We benchmark the approach on synthetic instances and realistic case studies, and implement it on the Fresnel quantum processor by Pasqal, solving instances of up to 100 nodes. Our results show that quantum-generated samples, despite hardware noise, enable near-optimal solutions of the placement problem. Overall, our results demonstrate that neutral-atom devices operating in analog mode can already be used to tackle graph optimization problems for real-world applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical framework using neutral-atom quantum computers as independent set samplers to solve the minimum dominating set problem for emergency operation center placement, achieving near-optimal solutions on instances up to 100 nodes using Pasqal's Fresnel processor.
AI.motivation: To address the problem of emergency operation center placement in disaster response, where minimal hubs must be selected to ensure timely coverage of all affected locations, formulated as a minimum dominating set problem.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical approximation framework using neutral-atom quantum computers as independent set samplers; candidate dominating sets are constructed from small maximal independent sets and complements of large independent sets, then refined via a lightweight classical procedure.
AI.result: Benchmarked on synthetic instances and realistic case studies, implemented on Pasqal's Fresnel quantum processor, solving instances up to 100 nodes. Quantum-generated samples enabled near-optimal solutions despite hardware noise.
AI.conclusion: Neutral-atom devices operating in analog mode can already be used to tackle graph optimization problems for real-world applications like disaster response hub placement.

title: Stalls and Spequlation: Pipelined Execution for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computation
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires the coordinated action of three distinct systems: classical control logic, quantum hardware, and classical error decoders. Current scheduling models treat logical operations as atomic, hiding the fact that these subsystems operate sequentially and spend significant time idle. We present a pipelined execution framework that decomposes each logical operation into its component stages i.e. Control, Execute, and Decode. Building on this, we discuss some speculation strategies that allow successor operations to begin processing before their predecessors have completed decoding. We evaluate our framework on several common benchmarks and show that pipelining with speculation reduces total pipeline steps by 20-40% compared to a no-speculation baseline. The most aggressive strategy consistently outperforms conservative alternatives, even though partial rollback is needed at times, because the per-rollback penalty is small relative to the parallelism gained. We further show that speculation facilitates load balancing by distributing work more evenly across the heterogeneous subsystems of a fault-tolerant quantum computer, converting idle time into useful computation while also saving on execution time.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a pipelined execution framework for fault-tolerant quantum computation that decomposes logical operations into Control, Execute, and Decode stages, and uses speculation strategies to overlap operations, achieving 20-40% reduction in pipeline steps and better load balancing across heterogeneous subsystems.
AI.motivation: Current scheduling models treat logical operations as atomic, hiding the fact that classical control, quantum hardware, and error decoders operate sequentially and spend significant time idle. The goal is to expose this structure and reduce idle time.
AI.method: The authors propose a pipelined execution framework that decomposes each logical operation into Control, Execute, and Decode stages. They introduce speculation strategies that allow successor operations to begin before predecessors finish decoding, and evaluate aggressive vs. conservative speculation with partial rollback.
AI.result: Pipelining with speculation reduces total pipeline steps by 20-40% compared to no-speculation baseline. The most aggressive strategy consistently outperforms conservative alternatives despite occasional partial rollback, as the per-rollback penalty is small relative to the parallelism gained. Speculation also facilitates load balancing across subsystems.
AI.conclusion: Speculative pipelining effectively converts idle time into useful computation, saves execution time, and balances workloads across the heterogeneous components of fault-tolerant quantum computers, making the approach viable for practical quantum computation scheduling.

title: String dynamics of a (2+1)D U(1) quantum link model on a digital quantum computer
summary: The (2+1)D U(1) pure gauge theory always exists in the confining phase, with strings of non-zero string tension giving a characteristic linear potential between static charges. This makes it a useful testing ground for quantum computing methods designed to study string dynamics of confining gauge theories. Here we implement a minimal U(1) quantum link model on a quantum computer with qubit degrees of freedom representing the dual height variables of the model. This facilitates an efficient realization of plaquette interactions and enables effective calculations of real-time dynamics that are inaccessible to traditional quantum Monte Carlo. A specifically tailored lattice geometry is chosen to match the heavy-hexagonal geometry of the IBM quantum hardware used here, minimizing non-adjacent qubit interactions. By performing quantum quenches from a simple initial string state, we probe the transverse quantum fluctuations of the string before it thermalizes. Our experimental results from digital quantum simulations, with up to 112 qubits, show good agreement with reference tensor-network calculations at short times and with thermal averages at long times. Near the phase transition, the quench dynamics exhibit large fluctuations of the initial string that extend across both spatial dimensions of the lattice. Nonetheless, our error-mitigated estimators from the quantum hardware also give accurate predictions in that regime, with noise-induced violations of local gauge symmetries comparable to finite-bond-dimension tensor-network results.

AI.tldr: The paper implements a (2+1)D U(1) quantum link model on IBM quantum hardware (up to 112 qubits) using dual height variables to study real-time string dynamics in confining gauge theories, with results validated against tensor-network calculations and thermal averages.
AI.motivation: To leverage quantum computing to study real-time string dynamics in confining gauge theories, which are inaccessible to traditional quantum Monte Carlo methods due to the sign problem.
AI.method: A minimal U(1) quantum link model is implemented on a quantum computer using qubit degrees of freedom representing dual height variables, with a tailored heavy-hexagonal lattice geometry matching IBM hardware to minimize non-adjacent qubit interactions. Quantum quenches from a simple initial string state are performed to probe transverse quantum fluctuations.
AI.result: Digital quantum simulations with up to 112 qubits show good agreement with tensor-network calculations at short times and thermal averages at long times. Near the phase transition, large string fluctuations extend across both spatial dimensions, with error-mitigated estimators yielding accurate predictions and gauge symmetry violations comparable to finite-bond-dimension tensor-network results.
AI.conclusion: The dual height variable encoding and tailored lattice geometry enable efficient real-time dynamics calculations on current quantum hardware, demonstrating that near-term quantum computers can provide reliable results for confining gauge theory dynamics even near phase transitions.

title: Subsystem Quantum Error Correction for Noisy Quantum Metrology
summary: Quantum error correction has been successfully applied to enhance the precision of parameter estimation in the presence of noise. Nonetheless, existing methods require a number of noiseless, controllable ancillae and lack efficient encoding and decoding procedures. In this Letter, we demonstrate that subsystem error correction provides a new direction that can substantially simplify the metrological protocol. We derive general conditions under which subsystem stabilizer codes achieve the Heisenberg limit and show that, for broad classes of noise, this can be realized by syndrome-free protocols using at most a single ancilla qubit. Furthermore, we extend this framework to dynamical error correction and show that Floquet codes can protect time-dependent metrological signals in reaching the Heisenberg limit.

AI.tldr: Subsystem error correction simplifies quantum metrology, achieving Heisenberg-limited precision with minimal ancillae and without syndrome measurements, and extends to dynamical error correction via Floquet codes.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum error correction for metrology requires many noiseless ancillae and lacks efficient encoding/decoding; this work seeks to simplify the protocol using subsystem codes.
AI.method: Derives general conditions for subsystem stabilizer codes to achieve Heisenberg limit; introduces syndrome-free protocols using at most one ancilla; extends to dynamical error correction with Floquet codes.
AI.result: Subsystem codes achieve Heisenberg-limited precision for broad noise classes; syndrome-free protocols work with a single ancilla qubit; Floquet codes protect time-dependent signals.
AI.conclusion: Subsystem error correction provides a practical route to Heisenberg-limited metrology with minimal resources, and Floquet codes enable protection of dynamical metrological signals.

title: Optimized Quantum States for Sensing in the Presence of Loss and Phase Noise
comment: The build is 8 pages, 5 figures (3 in the body, 2 in the End Matter)
summary: Squeezed vacuum lets gravitational-wave detectors and other quantum sensors surpass the standard quantum limit, and is optimal in the loss-limited regime; phase noise breaks this optimality. Numerically optimizing the quantum Fisher information across the loss and phase-noise landscape, we identify non-Gaussian states that outperform any Gaussian state. These fall into three classes: Fock-like, cubic-phase-like, and states with discrete rotational symmetry. Limiting the average number of photons in the input state to $\bar{n}=5$, with $1-η= 5\%$ photon loss and 200 mrad phase noise, the non-Gaussian advantage reaches up to 2.2 dB. Furthermore, we observe that the non-Gaussian advantage can persist even when the measurement strategy is homodyne detection.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates non-Gaussian quantum states that outperform squeezed vacuum (the optimal Gaussian state) in quantum sensing under realistic conditions combining loss and phase noise. For moderate photon numbers (ñ=5), 5% loss, and 200 mrad phase noise, non-Gaussian states achieve up to 2.2 dB advantage over Gaussian states, categorized into Fock-like, cubic-phase-like, and rotationally-symmetric states, with advantage persisting even under simple homodyne measurement.
AI.motivation: Squeezed vacuum is optimal for loss-limited quantum sensing but loses optimality when phase noise is present alongside loss. The authors aim to identify states that outperform Gaussian states in this more realistic mixed-noise regime.
AI.method: Numerical optimization of the quantum Fisher information across the loss and phase-noise parameter space, identifying non-Gaussian states that outperform any Gaussian state.
AI.result: Three classes of outperforming non-Gaussian states identified: Fock-like, cubic-phase-like, and states with discrete rotational symmetry. Under ñ=5, 5% loss, 200 mrad phase noise, the non-Gaussian advantage reaches 2.2 dB, and persists even under homodyne detection.
AI.conclusion: Non-Gaussian states offer a tangible advantage over optimal Gaussian states for quantum sensing in realistic noisy environments combining loss and phase noise, and this advantage is robust to simple measurement strategies.

title: Quantum Dynamics from Lax Pair Theory: A Reconstruction from Spectrum Preservation
summary: We reconstruct unitary quantum dynamics from a minimal axiomatic foundation built on Hilbert-space observables and isospectral evolution. The only dynamical assumption is that physical time evolution is a continuous one-parameter flow of Hermitian observables that preserves their spectra, i.e. the possible outcomes of measurement. We show that this assumption is already sufficient to force the Lax form of quantum dynamics. The Heisenberg equation, the time-dependent and time-independent Schrödinger equations, conservation laws, and good quantum numbers then follow as theorems rather than postulates. In this formulation, Lax pair theory supplies the missing dynamical bridge between the measurement structure of a Hilbert space and standard quantum evolution: the Hamiltonian is not assumed, but emerges as the generator required for an isospectral observable flow.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that unitary quantum dynamics can be reconstructed solely from the assumption that time evolution preserves the spectrum of observables (i.e., measurement outcomes are fixed), from which the Heisenberg equation, Schrödinger equations, conservation laws, and the Hamiltonian emerge as theorems rather than postulates, using Lax pair theory as the bridge.
AI.motivation: To derive the full framework of quantum dynamics (unitary evolution, Hamiltonian, Schrödinger/Heisenberg equations) from a minimal set of axioms, eliminating the need to postulate the Hamiltonian or the form of time evolution.
AI.method: The paper starts from the assumption that physical time evolution is a continuous one-parameter flow of Hermitian observables that preserves their spectra (isospectral evolution). Using Lax pair theory, it shows that this spectral-preservation condition forces the Lax form of dynamics, from which the Heisenberg equation, time-dependent and time-independent Schrödinger equations, and conservation laws follow as theorems.
AI.result: The isospectral assumption alone is sufficient to derive the Lax form of quantum dynamics. All standard quantum evolution equations (Heisenberg, Schrödinger) and the concept of the Hamiltonian emerge as derived consequences, not fundamental postulates.
AI.conclusion: Unitary quantum dynamics can be reconstructed from a minimal axiomatic foundation where the only dynamical axiom is spectrum preservation of observables. Lax pair theory provides the missing link between the measurement structure of Hilbert space and standard quantum evolution.

title: Topological Quantum Interferometry
summary: Structured light provides high-dimensional Hilbert spaces holding tremendous potential for fundamental quantum optics and quantum technologies. However, existing characterization methods, like Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference, typically assume perfectly tuned conditions, overlooking the geometric physics governing spatial mode evolution. Here, we establish topological quantum interferometry driven by an interaction-based geometric phase, the exchange Berry phase (BPX). Our formalism generalizes $q$-plate state generation and characterization to arbitrary topological charges and (de)tuning conditions, demonstrating that BPX acts as a geometric marker governing spatial interference. We show BPX serves as a deterministic control parameter, decomposing two-photon spatial patterns into geometry-dictated fundamental modes. This mapping reveals topological invariants and phase singularities that function as a non-tomographic witness for state dimensionality estimation, circumventing full-state reconstruction. Being device-independent and highly scalable, this approach enables scalable high-dimensional characterization and topologically protected state selection, with direct applicability to quantum metrology and high-capacity quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces topological quantum interferometry based on the exchange Berry phase (BPX) for characterizing structured light in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces, enabling non-tomographic dimensionality estimation and topologically protected state selection without requiring perfectly tuned conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing characterization methods like Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference assume perfectly tuned conditions and overlook the geometric physics governing spatial mode evolution, limiting their applicability to high-dimensional structured light systems.
AI.method: The authors establish a topological quantum interferometry framework driven by an interaction-based geometric phase (exchange Berry phase, BPX), generalizing q-plate state generation and characterization to arbitrary topological charges and (de)tuning conditions, and using BPX as a deterministic control parameter for decomposing two-photon spatial patterns.
AI.result: BPX acts as a geometric marker governing spatial interference, revealing topological invariants and phase singularities that function as a non-tomographic witness for state dimensionality estimation, circumventing full-state reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The approach is device-independent, highly scalable, and enables scalable high-dimensional characterization and topologically protected state selection, with direct applicability to quantum metrology and high-capacity quantum networks.

title: Sparse positive maps on qutrits with exact nondecomposability thresholds and PPT-entanglement transitions
summary: We study a family of sparse positive maps on qutrits for which positivity, decomposability, and PPT entanglement can all be analysed explicitly. The block structure of the associated Choi matrices reduces positivity to a Hermitian biquadratic form and leads to exact positivity boundaries for three representative parametric families. For the same families we determine the exact transition between decomposable and non-decomposable maps and construct associated PPT states of two classes. The first consists of witness-adapted deformations naturally tied to the non-decomposability analysis. The second consists of analytically tractable families whose full PPT-entangled branch is detected by fixed positive maps, yielding exact thresholds between separability and bound entanglement. For the trace-preserving subclass, we further compare positivity with a recent eigenvalue bound for 2-positive maps, thereby making the gap between positivity and higher-order positivity fully explicit within this family.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes sparse positive maps on qutrits, providing exact boundaries for positivity, decomposability, and PPT entanglement using the block structure of Choi matrices. It constructs explicit PPT entangled states and compares positivity with higher-order positivity bounds.
AI.motivation: To systematically study and precisely characterize the transition regions between positivity, decomposability, and PPT entanglement in families of sparse positive maps on qutrits, and to construct explicit examples of bound entangled states.
AI.method: The block structure of Choi matrices is used to reduce positivity to Hermitian biquadratic forms. Exact positivity boundaries are derived for three parametric families. Decomposable/non-decomposable transitions are determined analytically. Two classes of PPT states are constructed: witness-adapted deformations and analytically tractable families detected by fixed positive maps.
AI.result: Exact positivity boundaries and decomposability thresholds are obtained for the studied families. PPT entangled states are explicitly constructed, including those with exact separability/bound entanglement thresholds. A gap between positivity and 2-positivity is fully characterized for the trace-preserving subclass.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a fully explicit framework for understanding the hierarchy of positivity and entanglement detection in qutrit systems, bridging the gap between decomposable and non-decomposable maps and between positivity and higher-order positivity.

title: Robust Generation of Topological Biphoton Mode via Adiabatic Passage
summary: Topological waveguide arrays support robust mode propagation in the presence of fabrication imperfections, providing a significant advantage for on-chip quantum information processing. However, this robustness does not fully extend to nonlinear biphoton generation. Structural disorder can enhance the excitation of non-topological biphoton modes during nonlinear interactions, which degrades the quantum properties of the generated state. To overcome this limitation, we propose an adiabatic passage that connects an isolated site to a topological defect array. By initiating the nonlinear process in a strongly isolated regime, nonlinear coupling to unwanted modes is effectively suppressed, thereby preserving the Schmidt number of the generated state. The subsequent adiabatic connection facilitates the high fidelity transfer of the generated biphoton into the topological biphoton mode. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that, unlike conventional topological structures, the adiabatic scheme maintains both high biphoton fidelity and a unit Schmidt number in the presence of waveguide gap disorder. Furthermore, we show that this robustness extends to path entangled NOON states, achieving a near-unity quantum interference visibility. Our approach provides a practical design strategy for disorder-tolerant integrated quantum photonic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adiabatic passage scheme connecting an isolated site to a topological defect array to suppress nonlinear coupling to unwanted biphoton modes, preserving a unit Schmidt number and high fidelity under waveguide gap disorder, with robustness extending to path-entangled NOON states.
AI.motivation: Topological waveguide arrays offer robust mode propagation against fabrication imperfections, but this robustness doesn't extend to nonlinear biphoton generation—structural disorder excites non-topological biphoton modes, degrading quantum state properties.
AI.method: An adiabatic passage connects an isolated site to a topological defect array. The nonlinear process is initiated in a strongly isolated regime to suppress unwanted nonlinear coupling, followed by adiabatic connection to transfer the generated biphoton into the topological biphoton mode with high fidelity.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show that the adiabatic scheme maintains both high biphoton fidelity and a unit Schmidt number under waveguide gap disorder, and achieves near-unity quantum interference visibility for path-entangled NOON states.
AI.conclusion: The adiabatic approach provides a practical design strategy for disorder-tolerant integrated quantum photonic devices, overcoming the limitations of conventional topological structures in nonlinear biphoton generation.

title: QMCtwin: Master-Equation Simulation of Syndrome Statistics Beyond Pauli Noise
summary: As quantum error correction moves toward large-scale experimental implementations, decoder performance increasingly depends on how faithfully hardware noise is translated into syndrome statistics. Standard stabilizer workflows achieve scalability by replacing device dynamics with stochastic Pauli or detector-error models, but this compression can discard coherent phase information, nonunital drift, continuous-time effects of always-on couplings, and correlations generated by simultaneous Hamiltonian and dissipative evolution. Here we present QMCtwin, a sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo framework for master-equation simulation of QEC circuits, and apply it to a full syndrome-extraction round of a distance-$7$ rotated surface code with $97$ physical qubits. The open-system model includes realistic superconducting-device noise mechanisms such as relaxation, pure dephasing, coherent gate miscalibration, residual $ZZ$ crosstalk, and drive-qubit detuning. By directly estimating syndrome observables from the QMC-generated stochastic density matrix estimator, we compare the master-equation dynamics with their Pauli-twirled Clifford simulation counterparts. QMCtwin predicts syndrome-extraction biases and correlations between syndromes and proxies of logical-string-parity that are absent or strongly suppressed in the stochastic Pauli description. We introduce information-theoretic diagnostics that further quantify how information concerning syndromes versus string-parity proxies differs between the realistic master-equation simulation and the corresponding Pauli-twirled model. These results show that QMC-based master-equation digital twins can expose noise features hidden by conventional Pauli/Clifford noise models and provide a practical path toward more accurate decoder-facing syndrome models.

AI.tldr: QMCtwin is a sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo framework for master-equation simulation of QEC circuits that reveals syndrome-extraction biases and noise correlations in a distance-7 surface code that are hidden by standard Pauli/Clifford noise models, providing a path toward more accurate decoder-facing syndrome models.
AI.motivation: Standard stabilizer workflows replace device dynamics with stochastic Pauli or detector-error models for scalability, but this compression discards coherent phase information, nonunital drift, continuous-time effects, and correlations from simultaneous Hamiltonian and dissipative evolution, leading to inaccurate syndrome statistics for decoders.
AI.method: The authors present QMCtwin, a sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo framework for master-equation simulation of QEC circuits. They apply it to a full syndrome-extraction round of a distance-7 rotated surface code with 97 physical qubits, including realistic superconducting noise mechanisms (relaxation, pure dephasing, coherent gate miscalibration, residual ZZ crosstalk, drive-qubit detuning), and compare the master-equation dynamics with their Pauli-twirled Clifford simulation counterparts.
AI.result: QMCtwin predicts syndrome-extraction biases and correlations between syndromes and logical-string-parity proxies that are absent or strongly suppressed in the stochastic Pauli description. Information-theoretic diagnostics quantify how syndrome vs. string-parity proxy information differs between the master-equation simulation and the Pauli-twirled model.
AI.conclusion: QMC-based master-equation digital twins can expose noise features hidden by conventional Pauli/Clifford noise models and provide a practical path toward more accurate decoder-facing syndrome models for quantum error correction.

title: Random Local Stabilizer Codes in Three Dimensions without String or Self-Similar Fractal Logical Operators
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures. Repository for data: https://github.com/hanyanphysics/QTRCC
summary: Quantum error-correcting codes (QECs) are essential components quantum computation and have deep connections to quantum phases of matter. A key obstruction to passive self-correcting QECs is the presence of string logical operators, which can generate logical errors through constant-energy-barrier processes. Haah's Codes (fracton codes) showed that three-dimensional stabilizer codes can forbid such string logical operators, but their translation-invariant structure supports self-similar fractal logical operators with a logarithmic energy barrier. We introduce the qutrit random cubic codes, a family of local qutrit Calderbank-Shor-Steane stabilizer Hamiltonians with similar cube-check structure as Haah's Code 1 but built from spatially varying stabilizers. We prove that these models retain the no-string property and numerically observe that they have properties distinct from translation-invariant fracton codes: the smallest ground-state degeneracy exponent is $k=2$ for odd $L$ and $k=4$ for even $L$; noncontractible plane-logical operators span the entire logical space; and charge-push diagnostics show that the self-similar fractal operators are absent. These results demonstrate that constrained randomness can fundamentally change the nature of stabilizer codes and improve their self-correction properties. They further point to broader families of quantum error-correcting codes and quantum phases beyond canonical topological and fracton orders.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces qutrit random cubic codes, a family of 3D stabilizer Hamiltonians with spatially varying stabilizers, that eliminate string logical operators and self-similar fractal operators found in translation-invariant fracton codes like Haah's Code, achieving distinct ground-state degeneracy and improved self-correction properties.
AI.motivation: Quantum error-correcting codes suffer from string logical operators that cause logical errors via constant-energy-barrier processes, hindering passive self-correction. While Haah's fracton codes forbid string operators, their translation-invariant structure still supports self-similar fractal logical operators with only logarithmic energy barriers. The goal is to overcome these limitations and improve self-correction.
AI.method: The authors construct qutrit (three-level) random cubic codes—local CSS stabilizer Hamiltonians with cube-check stabilizers analogous to Haah's Code 1, but with spatially varying (random) stabilizer coefficients instead of translation-invariant ones. They prove the no-string property analytically and numerically study ground-state degeneracy, logical operator structure, and charge-push diagnostics.
AI.result: (1) The smallest ground-state degeneracy exponent is k=2 for odd system size L and k=4 for even L. (2) Noncontractible plane-logical operators span the entire logical space. (3) Charge-push diagnostics show that self-similar fractal logical operators are absent. (4) The no-string property is provably retained.
AI.conclusion: Constrained randomness (spatial variation) fundamentally changes the nature of stabilizer codes, eliminating self-similar fractal operators and improving self-correction properties beyond what translation-invariant fracton codes can achieve. This points to broader families of QECs and quantum phases beyond canonical topological and fracton orders.

title: Purity and bound energy in ancilla-assisted work extraction
summary: We investigate ancilla-assisted work extraction in quantum batteries from the perspective of bound energy and purity. We show that the bound energy of the reduced system provides a tight upper bound to the daemonic gain and that this bound is saturated for globally pure system--ancilla states. Motivated by this relation, we introduce a purity-based gain that qualitatively predicts the daemonic gain without requiring explicit optimization over measurements. We further introduce a protocol to analyze the role of dissipation and intrinsic interactions on daemonic gain. Under a collective environment, dissipation can dynamically generate and stabilize finite daemonic gain through environment-induced correlations. In interacting systems, level crossings and spectral restructuring strongly modify the attainable gain through their influence on the accessible bound energy. Our results demonstrate that daemonic gain is governed not only by correlations, but also by the spectral structure of the underlying Hamiltonian and information loss captured by bound energy and purity.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates ancilla-assisted work extraction (daemonic gain) in quantum batteries, showing that bound energy of the reduced system provides a tight upper bound on daemonic gain, saturated for globally pure states. A purity-based gain is introduced to predict daemonic gain without measurement optimization. Under collective dissipation, finite daemonic gain can be dynamically generated via environment-induced correlations. In interacting systems, level crossings and spectral restructuring modify gain through bound energy changes. The results highlight that daemonic gain is governed by correlations, Hamiltonian spectral structure, and information loss via bound energy and purity.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of ancilla-assisted work extraction in quantum batteries by linking daemonic gain to bound energy and purity, and to explore how dissipation and interactions affect this gain.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of the relationship between bound energy and daemonic gain; introduction of a purity-based gain metric; analysis of dissipation and interaction effects via a proposed protocol involving collective environments and interacting systems.
AI.result: Bound energy provides a tight upper bound on daemonic gain, saturated for globally pure system-ancilla states. Purity-based gain qualitatively predicts daemonic gain. Collective dissipation can dynamically generate and stabilize finite daemonic gain. Level crossings and spectral restructuring in interacting systems modify attainable gain via bound energy changes.
AI.conclusion: Daemonic gain is governed not only by correlations, but also by the spectral structure of the underlying Hamiltonian and information loss captured by bound energy and purity.

title: QMaxCal: Path-Space Regularization for Open Quantum Control via Girsanov's Theorem
summary: Reliable quantum control in the presence of decoherence requires policies that combat the effect of environmental noise on the controlled dynamics. Open quantum systems under continuous monitoring generate classical measurement records whose drift depends on the noise experienced by the system; the records of two evolutions sharing the same decoherence channels differ only in this drift, so Girsanov's theorem yields a closed-form, differentiable estimator of the KL divergence between their trajectory distributions. We instantiate this estimator with two physically motivated reference measures, yielding two regularizers that both drive the system toward states where the effects of decoherence are minimal: the Wiener KL (KL_W), which is empirically more effective under certain conditions on the noise model, and the drift-variance regularizer (R_DV), which works for all noise models. Both are qualitatively distinct from existing penalties on control fluence or smoothness: they penalize the observable consequences of control on the decoherence channels rather than the control amplitude itself.
