The regularizers outperform unregularized gradient-based and reinforcement-learning baselines across a range of open quantum systems -- including single- and multi-qubit benchmarks and a multi-qubit chain calibrated to a published snapshot of the IBM Kingston processor -- along several axes of evaluation: final-state fidelity, robustness to mismatch in the assumed noise model (gains grow from +17 pp at training noise to +27 pp under 2.5x noise mismatch), and occupation of forbidden states. The regularizers reduce infidelity by up to 50%, with ~16% gains on the calibrated IBM Kingston chain.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two differentiable regularizers (Wiener KL and drift-variance) derived from Girsanov's theorem to minimize decoherence effects in open quantum systems under continuous monitoring. These regularizers penalize the observable consequences of control on decoherence channels rather than control amplitude, outperforming unregularized baselines in fidelity, noise-robustness, and forbidden-state occupation across single/multi-qubit benchmarks and a calibrated IBM Kingston processor chain.
AI.motivation: Reliable quantum control in the presence of decoherence requires policies that combat environmental noise. Existing regularizers penalize control fluence or smoothness rather than the actual consequences of control on decoherence channels, motivating the need for physically grounded regularizers that directly target decoherence effects.
AI.method: Using Girsanov's theorem, the authors derive a closed-form, differentiable KL divergence estimator between trajectory distributions of open quantum systems under continuous monitoring. They instantiate two regularizers: Wiener KL (KL_W) and drift-variance (R_DV), which penalize observable consequences of control on decoherence channels. These are evaluated against gradient-based and reinforcement-learning baselines.
AI.result: Regularizers outperform baselines across single/multi-qubit benchmarks and a multi-qubit chain calibrated to IBM Kingston processor. Gains include +17 to +27 pp fidelity under noise mismatch, up to 50% infidelity reduction, and ~16% gains on the IBM Kingston chain. KL_W is more effective under certain noise conditions; R_DV works for all noise models.
AI.conclusion: Physically motivated regularizers that penalize decoherence consequences rather than control amplitude yield significant improvements in quantum control fidelity, noise robustness, and forbidden-state avoidance, demonstrating effectiveness even on real-world calibrated quantum hardware (IBM Kingston).

title: Majorana bound states in a hybrid Kitaev ladder with long-range pairing
comment: 11 pages, 11 figures, Submitted for review at Phys. Rev. B
summary: We investigate an inter-leg coupled hybrid Kitaev ladder composed of two parallel superconducting chains with distinct pairing interactions. The upper chain of the ladder hosts conventional $p$-wave pairing, while the lower chain exhibits long-range pairing that decays algebraically with distance. We demonstrate that the mutual influence of long-range pairing exponent, chemical potential, and inter-leg coupling strength gives rise to a rich topological phase diagram characterized by multiple Majorana zero modes and massive Dirac modes. In particular, we show that the inter-leg coupling renormalizes the effective energy scales, leading to a systematic shift of the topological phase boundaries and enabling controlled tuning of the Majorana modes. Furthermore, we identify a transition from a two Majorana zero mode phase to a phase encapsulating four Majorana zero modes, as the long-range pairing exponent is varied. This transition is accompanied by a crossover regime in which Majorana zero modes coexist with massive Dirac modes, reflecting hybridization between edge and bulk excitations. This ladder thus provides a minimal and attractive platform for realizing the impact of a long-range pairing on topological phases. Our results highlight the potential of long-range hybrid systems for engineering tunable topological states relevant for quantum information applications.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a hybrid Kitaev ladder with one chain having conventional p-wave pairing and the other having long-range pairing, revealing a rich topological phase diagram with multiple Majorana zero modes and massive Dirac modes, including a transition from two to four Majorana zero modes controlled by the long-range pairing exponent.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between long-range pairing and inter-leg coupling in a minimal ladder system, and to explore how these factors can tune topological phases and Majorana modes for potential quantum information applications.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of an inter-leg coupled hybrid Kitaev ladder with two parallel superconducting chains (one with conventional p-wave pairing, the other with algebraically decaying long-range pairing), varying the long-range pairing exponent, chemical potential, and inter-leg coupling strength.
AI.result: The inter-leg coupling renormalizes effective energy scales, shifting topological phase boundaries. A transition from a two-Majorana to a four-Majorana zero mode phase occurs as the long-range pairing exponent varies, with a crossover regime where Majorana zero modes coexist with massive Dirac modes.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid Kitaev ladder provides a minimal platform for realizing and tuning topological phases via long-range pairing, highlighting its potential for engineering tunable topological states for quantum information.

title: On chip, multifunctional quantum sensing using single spins in a van der Waals crystal
summary: Nanoscale thermometry and magnetometry are in high demand across a wide range of scientific and technological applications. In this context, optically addressable spins in solids have emerged at the forefront of on-chip quantum sensing. However, simultaneous quantum sensing of multiple parameters (e.g., temperature and magnetic field) using the same spin sensor remains challenging due to cross-sensitivity to multiple physical quantities. Here, we demonstrate independent dual sensing of temperature and magnetic field using single quantum emitters in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). We experimentally verify the independent response of the zero-phonon line (ZPL) position to temperature and of optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) to magnetic fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate local temperature sensing of a microcircuit while simultaneously measuring an external magnetic field. Our results establish quantum emitters in hBN as a robust platform for multifunctional quantum sensing under realistic operating conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates independent dual sensing of temperature and magnetic field using single quantum emitters in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), leveraging zero-phonon line (ZPL) position for temperature and optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) for magnetic field measurements simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Simultaneous quantum sensing of multiple parameters (e.g., temperature and magnetic field) using the same spin sensor is challenging due to cross-sensitivity to multiple physical quantities. There is a need for a platform that can independently measure multiple parameters.
AI.method: The authors use single quantum emitters in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) as quantum sensors. They experimentally verify the independent response of the zero-phonon line (ZPL) position to temperature and optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) to magnetic fields, enabling dual-parameter sensing without cross-talk.
AI.result: The independent response of ZPL to temperature and ODMR to magnetic fields is experimentally verified. Local temperature sensing of a microcircuit is demonstrated while simultaneously measuring an external magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: Quantum emitters in hBN are established as a robust platform for multifunctional quantum sensing under realistic operating conditions, enabling simultaneous independent measurement of temperature and magnetic fields.

title: Optimal Shadow Estimation with Minimal Measurement Settings
comment: 8+21 pages and 3+5 figures; comments and suggestions are very welcome!
summary: Shadow estimation is a powerful framework for predicting quantum properties from randomized measurements. While $3$-design protocols achieve optimal worst-case performance, the minimal number of measurement bases required for such optimality has remained open. Here we prove that $Θ(d^2)$ measurement bases are both necessary and sufficient for worst-case optimal shadow estimation and construct an explicit basis family. In stark contrast, any state $2$-design already suffices for average-case optimality: the mean squared shadow norm of normalized observables is bounded by a universal constant, and we prove strong concentration for Haar-random states, yielding constant sample complexity for generic pure-state fidelity estimation. Easily implementable $2$-designs -- from mutually unbiased bases, cyclic measurements, or shallow $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-depth circuits -- enable optimal average-case protocols with remarkably simple measurement strategies. Our results establish a fundamental complexity separation: worst-case estimation requires $Θ(d^2)$ bases, whereas average-case performance requires only $Θ(d)$ bases, with broad implications for quantum information theory and near-term experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that worst-case optimal shadow estimation requires Θ(d²) measurement bases, while average-case optimality only needs Θ(d) bases (achievable with any state 2-design). This establishes a fundamental complexity separation between worst-case and average-case quantum state shadow estimation.
AI.motivation: To resolve the open problem of the minimal number of measurement bases required for worst-case optimal shadow estimation, and to understand the gap between worst-case and average-case performance in quantum shadow estimation protocols.
AI.method: The authors prove necessity and sufficiency of Θ(d²) measurement bases for worst-case optimal shadow estimation via explicit basis construction; they analyze average-case performance using state 2-designs, bounding the mean squared shadow norm and proving concentration for Haar-random states.
AI.result: Θ(d²) measurement bases are both necessary and sufficient for worst-case optimal shadow estimation; any state 2-design suffices for average-case optimality with constant sample complexity for generic pure-state fidelity estimation; easily implementable 2-designs (MUBs, cyclic measurements, shallow O(log n)-depth circuits) enable optimal average-case protocols.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental complexity separation: worst-case estimation requires Θ(d²) bases while average-case performance requires only Θ(d) bases, with broad implications for quantum information theory and near-term experiments.

title: The use of Peres lattices in periodically driven systems
summary: We demonstrate the strength of the method of Peres lattices in periodically driven quantum systems. The method, which has previously been used mostly in stationary systems, enables us to efficiently detect resonances in the driven system, to monitor the onset of chaos, and to recognize critical properties of the Floquet modes. It also allows quick comparisons of the spectra of Floquet modes for various driving Hamiltonians and transparent tests of the iterative approximation techniques based on effective stationary Hamiltonians.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that Peres lattices, previously used mainly in stationary systems, are effective tools for analyzing periodically driven quantum systems—detecting resonances, monitoring chaos onset, recognizing critical properties of Floquet modes, comparing spectra across driving Hamiltonians, and testing iterative approximation techniques based on effective stationary Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: To extend the Peres lattice method—traditionally applied to stationary quantum systems—to periodically driven quantum systems, enabling better detection of resonances, chaos, and critical properties of Floquet modes.
AI.method: Application of Peres lattices to periodically driven quantum systems; the method constructs lattice representations to visualize and analyze Floquet mode properties, resonance structures, and chaos onset.
AI.result: The method efficiently detects resonances, monitors chaos onset, recognizes critical Floquet mode properties, enables quick spectral comparisons across different driving Hamiltonians, and provides transparent tests of iterative approximation techniques based on effective stationary Hamiltonians.
AI.conclusion: Peres lattices are a powerful and versatile tool for analyzing periodically driven quantum systems, extending their utility beyond stationary systems.

title: All-valid-state HOBO encoding for constrained combinatorial optimization on NISQ devices
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures. Corresponding author: Jun-ichi Shirakashi
summary: Continued advancements in quantum computing have stimulated growing interest in translating quantum technologies into real-world applications. Consequently, the investigation of practically motivated NP-hard problems is of significant value. This study investigates the performance of a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) in addressing the traveling salesperson problem (TSP) through noiseless simulations representative of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices using higher-order binary optimization (HOBO) encodings. We construct a HOBO Hamiltonian with an efficient binary representation and propose an all-valid-state HOBO (AVS-HOBO) scheme based on cyclic mapping that eliminates one penalty term and reuses states that would otherwise be invalid. Using TSP instances of up to 20 cities, we compare the original HOBO and AVS-HOBO encodings from multiple perspectives, including the energy convergence behavior and the approximation, tour-length, and feasibility ratios. In addition to simulations, we perform computations on real quantum hardware with different device architectures, where we not only compare the performances of different chips but also investigate the effects of different error-mitigation methods on actual quantum machines. The results indicate that AVS-HOBO encoding enhances the practical reliability of VQE on NISQ devices and improves scalability for larger TSP instances, with broader applicability to constrained quantum optimization problems.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) using Higher-Order Binary Optimization (HOBO) encodings, proposes an All-Valid-State HOBO (AVS-HOBO) scheme based on cyclic mapping, and demonstrates via noiseless simulations (up to 20 cities) and real quantum hardware experiments that AVS-HOBO improves reliability and scalability on NISQ devices.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing advances drive interest in real-world applications; investigating practically motivated NP-hard problems like TSP is valuable for translating quantum technologies into practice.
AI.method: Constructed a HOBO Hamiltonian with efficient binary representation; proposed AVS-HOBO scheme using cyclic mapping to eliminate one penalty term and reuse invalid states. Compared original HOBO vs. AVS-HOBO via noiseless NISQ simulations (up to 20 cities) and real quantum hardware experiments across different device architectures with various error-mitigation methods.
AI.result: AVS-HOBO encoding enhances practical reliability of VQE on NISQ devices and improves scalability for larger TSP instances, with better energy convergence, approximation, tour-length, and feasibility ratios compared to original HOBO.
AI.conclusion: AVS-HOBO encoding improves the practical reliability and scalability of VQE for constrained quantum optimization problems on NISQ devices, with broader applicability beyond TSP.

title: Simulation of Non-Markovian Quantum Accelerated Dynamics via Time-Fractional Schrödinger Equation
summary: The Time-Fractional Schrödinger Equation (TFSE) is an effective tool for simulating the dynamics of non-Markovian quantum systems. The Quantum Speed Limit (QSL) time characterizes the minimum time required for the evolution of a non-Markovian quantum system. In this paper, Wei's TFSE is employed to simulate the non-Markovian quantum accelerated evolution process in the Resonant Dissipative Jaynes-Cummings (RDJC) model. By solving the QSL time of a time-fractional single-qubit open system, the enhancement mechanism of the system evolution speed induced by the non-Markovian memory effects of the environment is revealed. Further studies show that the optimized acceleration of the system evolution can be achieved by jointly regulating the fractional order, coupling strength, and photon number. Comparative analyses indicate that Wei's TFSE can accurately capture the non-Markovian accelerated dynamical features of the system over the entire fractional order range, whereas Naber's TFSE is applicable only within a limited fractional order interval. In addition, the comparisons of the average simulation time for calculating the dynamical trajectory of the excited-state probability demonstrate that Wei's TFSE has a significant simulation advantage in computational efficiency. Therefore, Wei's TFSE is more accurate and efficient for simulating the accelerated dynamics of non-Markovian quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Wei's Time-Fractional Schrödinger Equation (TFSE) to simulate non-Markovian quantum accelerated evolution in the RDJC model, showing it offers superior accuracy and efficiency over Naber's TFSE for capturing system acceleration dynamics across the full fractional order range.
AI.motivation: To effectively simulate the dynamics of non-Markovian quantum systems and understand the enhancement mechanism of system evolution speed induced by non-Markovian memory effects of the environment.
AI.method: Wei's TFSE is employed to simulate non-Markovian accelerated evolution in the RDJC model; the QSL time of a time-fractional single-qubit open system is solved; joint regulation of fractional order, coupling strength, and photon number is explored; comparative analysis against Naber's TFSE is performed.
AI.result: Wei's TFSE accurately captures non-Markovian accelerated dynamics over the entire fractional order range, while Naber's TFSE is only applicable within a limited interval. Wei's TFSE also demonstrates significant computational efficiency advantage in average simulation time for excited-state probability trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Wei's TFSE is more accurate and efficient for simulating accelerated dynamics of non-Markovian quantum systems compared to Naber's TFSE.

title: QPU-scale randomized benchmarking via Bell-pair injection
comment: Haripriya Pettugani, María Aguado-Yáñez and Astryd Park contributed equally to this work
summary: Mirror randomized benchmarking (MRB) is an established technique that provides a global error metric at the scale of a whole QPU. To expand upon this we introduce Mirror Quantum Awesomeness (MQA), a hybrid protocol that adds a structured entangling layer to MRB circuits. This enables per-edge correlation dynamics to be tracked via mutual information while preserving the MRB infidelity estimate. The resulting analysis of the injected entangled pairs locates a critical circuit depth, beyond which rudimentary error mitigation techniques can be expected to fail. A topological variant, Topological MQA, supplies a second critical depth via a decoder based on the surface-code decoding problem. Both are validated in simulation and demonstrated on the 156-qubit \texttt{ibm\_fez} and \texttt{ibm\_kingston} processors, where MQA closely agrees with MRB on the entanglement infidelity and the critical depth for \texttt{ibm\_fez} is found to be $\sim 50$.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mirror Quantum Awesomeness (MQA), a hybrid benchmarking protocol that adds structured entangling layers to Mirror Randomized Benchmarking (MRB) circuits. MQA tracks per-edge correlation dynamics via mutual information while preserving MRB's infidelity estimates, identifies a critical circuit depth beyond which error mitigation fails, and includes a topological variant (Topological MQA) that provides a second critical depth via surface-code decoding. Validated on 156-qubit IBM processors, MQA closely agrees with MRB on entanglement infidelity and finds a critical depth of ~50 for ibm_fez.
AI.motivation: To expand upon MRB's global error metric by introducing a hybrid protocol that tracks per-edge correlation dynamics and identifies critical depths where error mitigation techniques fail.
AI.method: MQA adds structured entangling layers to MRB circuits, tracks correlation dynamics via mutual information, and includes a topological variant using surface-code decoding to identify two critical depths.
AI.result: Validated on 156-qubit ibm_fez and ibm_kingston processors; MQA closely agrees with MRB on entanglement infidelity; critical depth for ibm_fez is ~50.
AI.conclusion: MQA provides richer benchmarking insight than MRB alone, identifying critical depths for error mitigation failure and offering a topological variant for additional decoding-based depth analysis.

title: Optimizing resource allocation for accuracy in noisy variational quantum algorithms
summary: For quantum algorithms to achieve their full potential, we need methodologies to optimize them, such as reaching a given output accuracy with minimal resource costs. Here, we develop such a methodology for a class of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) algorithms. We leverage simulations of a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) to propose a phenomenological model of such algorithms that captures the complex relationship between algorithmic accuracy, algorithmic resource costs, and the noise that exists in realistic quantum hardware. For this, we take the algorithmic resource cost to be the total number of quantum gate-operations in the algorithm; minimizing this cost typically makes the algorithm faster and more energy-efficient. We consider the subtle trade-off between quantum circuit size (small circuits are too imprecise, but large ones are too noisy), and the number of iterations of that quantum circuit for the full algorithm to sufficiently converge. Using a noise-metric-resource methodology, we identify the sweet spot (of circuit size versus iterations) that minimizes the algorithmic resource costs for a desired algorithm accuracy. It also gives the circuit size that maximizes algorithm accuracy for a fixed resource cost. Our methodology provides a practical guideline for near-term deployment of variational algorithms on realistic noisy hardware, including hardware that uses error mitigation.

AI.tldr: Develops a noise-metric-resource methodology for NISQ variational algorithms that identifies the optimal trade-off between quantum circuit size and number of iterations to minimize resource costs for a given accuracy, or maximize accuracy for fixed resources.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithms need optimization methodologies to achieve full potential, specifically reaching target output accuracy with minimal resource costs—a critical gap for practical NISQ deployment.
AI.method: Uses VQE simulations to build a phenomenological model relating algorithmic accuracy, resource costs (total number of quantum gate operations), and hardware noise. Analyzes trade-off between circuit size (small=imprecise, large=noisy) and iteration count, then applies a noise-metric-resource methodology to find optimal operating points.
AI.result: Identifies the sweet spot of circuit size versus iterations that minimizes algorithmic resource costs for a desired accuracy, and the circuit size that maximizes accuracy for a fixed resource cost.
AI.conclusion: Provides a practical guideline for deploying variational algorithms on near-term noisy quantum hardware, including hardware using error mitigation.

title: Multi-objective design of photon blockade for bright single-photon sources
summary: High-quality single-photon sources, realized through saturable emitters, photon blockade, or heralded pair generation, are indispensable building blocks for photonic quantum platforms. Although these mechanisms suppress multiphoton emission through distinct principles typically captured by analytical models, their practical implementation is constrained by conflicting requirements for purity, brightness, and indistinguishability, which must be balanced within high-dimensional design landscapes. Here, we propose a computational framework for optimizing competing metrics of single-photon sources. Building on a Liouville-space adjoint formulation that efficiently evaluates multiple objectives in Markovian open quantum systems, we develop a Jacobian-based update, which ensures first-order monotonic reduction of multi-objective costs. By incorporating simulated annealing to escape gradient-vanishing plateaus, our framework achieves a design success rate of nearly 60 % for photon blockade with g2(0) smaller than 0.1 and theoretically bounded brightness across a broad parameter space, without any analytical guidance. This framework provides a general recipe for multi-objective design of open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A computational framework using Liouville-space adjoint method and Jacobian-based updates with simulated annealing optimizes multi-objective metrics (purity, brightness, indistinguishability) for single-photon sources, achieving ~60% design success rate for photon blockade without analytical guidance.
AI.motivation: Single-photon sources face conflicting requirements between purity, brightness, and indistinguishability that must be balanced in high-dimensional design spaces, lacking a general optimization framework.
AI.method: Liouville-space adjoint formulation for multi-objective evaluation in Markovian open quantum systems, Jacobian-based update for first-order monotonic cost reduction, and simulated annealing to escape gradient-vanishing plateaus.
AI.result: ~60% design success rate for photon blockade with g^(2)(0) < 0.1 and theoretically bounded brightness across broad parameter space, without analytical guidance.
AI.conclusion: Provides a general recipe for multi-objective design of open quantum systems.

title: Applications of quantum annealing to magnetic dipole hyperfine structure constants: First results beyond energies for atoms
summary: We report the first results of the magnetic dipole hyperfine structure (HFS) constants of neutral $\mathrm{Li}$, Li-like $\mathrm{Be}$, neutral $\mathrm{Na}$, and Na-like $\mathrm{Mg}$ using a modified version of the Quantum Annealer Eigensolver (QAE) algorithm on D-Wave's quantum hardware. The results are benchmarked against relativistic configuration interaction with multiconfiguration Dirac Hartree-Fock (MCDHF) calculations using the General-purpose Relativistic Atomic Structure Package (GRASP), and simulated annealing. In our modified QAE, a zooming-and-sigma-annealing approach with a floating-point encoding scheme is adopted to estimate the ground-state eigenvalue and eigenvector of the relativistic Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian matrices ($H_{\mathrm{DC}}$) constructed from 11 or fewer configuration state functions (CSFs). For calculations with extended correlation orbital sets, we applied a CSF truncation scheme, retaining only CSFs (up to 12) that make significant contributions to the ground-state wavefunction. Our modified QAE precision is kept limited to three decimal places (up to 10 qubits). Hardware demonstrations on the D-Wave quantum processing unit (QPU) yielded results that were completely consistent with GRASP (at the chosen precision) in determining the magnetic dipole HFS constants, with accuracy varying across systems and $H_{\mathrm{DC}}$ matrix dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents first results of magnetic dipole hyperfine structure constants for Li, Be+, Na, and Mg+ using a modified Quantum Annealer Eigensolver (QAE) algorithm on D-Wave quantum hardware, benchmarked against GRASP/MCDHF calculations, achieving consistent results at 3-decimal precision with up to 10 qubits.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the viability of quantum annealing hardware for accurately computing atomic hyperfine structure constants, an important quantum chemistry problem, by modifying the QAE algorithm to handle relativistic Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian matrices.
AI.method: Modified QAE algorithm with zooming-and-sigma-annealing approach and floating-point encoding scheme; CSF truncation scheme (retaining up to 12 CSFs); relativistic Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian matrices constructed from ≤11 CSFs; D-Wave QPU hardware demonstrations; benchmarked against GRASP/MCDHF and simulated annealing.
AI.result: Hardware results on D-Wave QPU were completely consistent with GRASP at the chosen precision (3 decimal places, up to 10 qubits) for magnetic dipole HFS constants, with accuracy varying across systems and Hamiltonian matrix dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Quantum annealing on D-Wave hardware can successfully reproduce relativistic atomic structure calculations for hyperfine constants at limited precision, demonstrating a viable quantum computing approach for atomic physics problems.

title: Quantum-Accelerated Self-Consistent Field: A Hybrid Algorithm
summary: We present the Grover adaptive search self-consistent field (GAS-SCF) algorithm. GAS-SCF leverages quantum arithmetic to construct an efficient oracle that marks target states (Fock states) which improve upon some initial classical energy estimate. Amplitude amplification then increases the probability of measuring these states. This approach offers a theoretical quadratic speed-up for the optimization problem encountered in SCF quantum chemistry and establishes a baseline against which structured optimization algorithms, such as QAOA and DQI may be compared. In this work, we classically simulate three examples as proofs of concept of the algorithm, the largest consisting of 26 qubits. We then extend our analysis to two larger systems, with O3 representing the largest case at 330 qubits. These examples are chosen to probe classically challenging SCF regimes. Achieving chemically relevant applications of GAS-SCF will require large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GAS-SCF, a quantum algorithm that uses Grover's search and amplitude amplification to achieve quadratic speed-up for self-consistent field optimization in quantum chemistry, demonstrated through classical simulations up to 26 qubits and analyzed up to 330 qubits (O3 case).
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum algorithm that accelerates the self-consistent field optimization problem in quantum chemistry, which is a computationally challenging step in electronic structure calculations.
AI.method: GAS-SCF combines quantum arithmetic to construct an oracle marking improved Fock states, then applies amplitude amplification (Grover's algorithm) to increase measurement probability of these target states, offering quadratic speed-up over classical SCF optimization.
AI.result: Classical simulations of up to 26 qubits demonstrated proof of concept; analysis extended to larger systems up to 330 qubits (O3). The algorithm establishes a baseline for comparison with structured optimization algorithms like QAOA and DQI.
AI.conclusion: GAS-SCF offers theoretical quadratic speed-up for SCF optimization but requires large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum hardware for chemically relevant applications.

title: Operator Learning for efficient Quantum Computation
summary: An efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is often hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation. This limits both the ability of near-term quantum hardware to simulate complex problems and the potential of fault-tolerant algorithms to achieve practical quantum advantage. To address this, we propose a full-stack variational framework that transforms arbitrary operators to compact quantum circuits. The resulting variational circuits can be tailored to the connectivity and long-range interaction of the target hardware. The learning process employs backpropagation together with a cost function that efficiently optimizes unitary operators and non-unitary -- dense or sparse -- operators using only a single ancilla qubit for block encoding. Additionally, we introduce a regularization term that reduces the approximation error. The approach is validated for both quantum mechanical and engineering applications. In the former case, we learn propagators that arise in native quantum problems -- such as quantum simulation and quantum chemistry -- and achieve improved resource scaling in comparison to standard Suzuki-Trotter expansions. In the latter case, we demonstrate the approach's ability to implement the second-order central finite difference approximation of the Laplace operator -- relevant for solving partial differential equations -- while improving upon current error metrics. The final example deals with learning a dense, non-unitary operator that arises in the analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil. This universality of the framework opens the door for solving general problems beyond prototypical engineering and quantum applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a full-stack variational framework that transforms arbitrary operators (unitary and non-unitary) into compact quantum circuits using backpropagation and a single ancilla qubit for block encoding, with a regularization term to reduce approximation error. The approach is validated on quantum simulation, quantum chemistry, finite difference Laplace operators, and potential flow problems, showing improved resource scaling and error metrics.
AI.motivation: Efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation, limiting both near-term quantum hardware and fault-tolerant algorithms from achieving practical quantum advantage.
AI.method: A full-stack variational framework that transforms arbitrary operators to compact quantum circuits, tailored to target hardware connectivity and long-range interactions. Uses backpropagation with a cost function that optimizes unitary and non-unitary (dense or sparse) operators using a single ancilla qubit for block encoding, plus a regularization term to reduce approximation error.
AI.result: Validated on quantum simulation and quantum chemistry (learned propagators with improved resource scaling over Suzuki-Trotter expansions), engineering applications (second-order central finite difference Laplace operator with improved error metrics), and analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil (learning a dense non-unitary operator).
AI.conclusion: The framework is universal, opening the door for solving general problems beyond prototypical engineering and quantum applications.

title: Optimal multi-spectral squeezing via deterministic 2D-phase optimization
summary: Optimization routines are ubiquitous in quantum information technologies and essential to reach the resource levels required by quantum protocols. Specifically, multi-spectral squeezing for use in such protocols requires that losses be kept minimal at every stage, including coherent detection, which is performed by interfering the signal with a classical local-oscillator beam. This in turn requires control over all optical degrees of freedom of the beam in order to optimize the detection. The most general framework for this optimization relies on agnostic, off-the-shelf machine-learning techniques. Here we take the opposite approach: by focusing on a physical description of the specific optical process, we develop a deterministic sequential algorithm that provably reaches the global maximum of the visibility in a pixel basis and scales linearly with the number of pixels, thereby offering an efficient and theoretically grounded alternative to black-box optimization. In our waveguide-based setup, the optimized mask increases the visibility from 76% to 84%, corresponding to a 20% gain in mode-matching efficiency. Multi-spectral squeezing measurements confirm that this improvement translates directly into quantum readout: for the most squeezed spectral mode, the squeezing increases from $-2.08$ dB to $-2.64$ dB, consistent with the inferred efficiency gain. These results establish deterministic spatial phase shaping as an effective, interpretable route to enhanced multimode squeezing in waveguide platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a deterministic sequential algorithm for optimizing spatial phase masks to improve mode-matching efficiency in multi-spectral squeezing experiments, achieving a 20% gain in mode-matching efficiency and increased squeezing from -2.08 dB to -2.64 dB, as an alternative to black-box machine-learning optimization.
AI.motivation: Optimization routines are essential for quantum information technologies, but existing approaches rely on agnostic machine-learning techniques. The authors aim to provide a more interpretable, theoretically grounded alternative for optimizing coherent detection in multi-spectral squeezing setups by leveraging physical understanding of the optical process.
AI.method: The authors develop a deterministic sequential algorithm based on a physical description of the optical process, operating in a pixel basis with linear scaling in the number of pixels. This algorithm provably reaches the global maximum of visibility and is tested in a waveguide-based setup with an optimized spatial phase mask.
AI.result: The optimized mask increased visibility from 76% to 84%, a 20% gain in mode-matching efficiency. Multi-spectral squeezing measurements showed increased squeezing from -2.08 dB to -2.64 dB for the most squeezed spectral mode, consistent with the efficiency gain.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic spatial phase shaping offers an effective, interpretable alternative to black-box optimization for enhancing multimode squeezing in waveguide platforms, providing theoretically grounded and efficient optimization.

title: Random Projections for Multi-Copy Quantum Algorithms
comment: 5 pages + End Matter (2 pages) + Supplemental Materials (20 pages); 4 + 8 figures
summary: Estimating nonlinear properties of quantum states is a central task in quantum information science. Multivariate traces, $\mathrm{tr}(ρ_1 \cdots ρ_K)$, and nonlinear observables such as $\mathrm{tr}(ρ^K)$, for integer $K$, can be accessed through collective measurements on multiple state copies, but standard protocols based on swap tests require coherent operations on the full Hilbert space and become experimentally unfeasible for large systems. In this work, we introduce a framework for multi-copy measurements based on random projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces prior to the collective measurement, which is then performed only on the reduced Hilbert space. This procedure yields a tunable tradeoff between coherent quantum resources and statistical sampling overhead, allowing the amount of coherent processing to be matched to the capabilities of the underlying hardware. We derive explicit formulas relating the Haar-averaged projected moments to multivariate traces of the original states and analyze the sampling overhead induced by the projection procedure. Specifically, after compressing an $n$-qubit state to a reduced $q$-qubit subspace, estimating $\mathrm{tr}(ρ^K)$ requires approximately $O(2^{(n-q)(K-1)})$ copies of $ρ$, with each qubit projected out increasing the sampling cost by a factor of $2^{K-1}$. Our results establish how coherent multi-copy operations can be traded for additional state copies, enabling multi-copy quantum protocols to be optimized for the available hardware resources.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for multi-copy quantum measurements that uses random projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces before collective measurements, enabling a tunable tradeoff between coherent quantum resources and statistical sampling overhead. Compressing an n-qubit state to a q-qubit subspace increases sampling cost by a factor of ~2^{(n-q)(K-1)} for estimating tr(ρ^K).
AI.motivation: Estimating nonlinear properties like multivariate traces and tr(ρ^K) is essential in quantum information, but standard swap-test-based protocols require coherent operations on the full Hilbert space, which becomes experimentally infeasible for large systems. The goal is to develop a method that reduces coherent resource requirements while managing the statistical overhead.
AI.method: The authors propose performing random projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces before collective measurements, limiting coherent operations to the reduced Hilbert space. They derive analytical formulas for Haar-averaged projected moments relating to multivariate traces, and analyze the sampling overhead as a function of the compression ratio.
AI.result: Estimating tr(ρ^K) after compressing from n qubits to q qubits requires ~O(2^{(n-q)(K-1)}) copies of ρ; each projected-out qubit increases sampling cost by 2^{K-1}. This establishes a quantitative tradeoff between coherent resources and sampling overhead.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables multi-copy quantum protocols to be optimized for available hardware by tuning the projection dimension, effectively trading coherent operations for additional state copies.

title: Mitigating Trotter Errors via Post-Processed Symmetry Restoration
summary: Quantum simulation is a powerful tool for exploring complex quantum many-body systems such as condensed matter physics and gauge theories. Trotterization, which approximates the ideal time evolution operator by decomposing it into a sequence of local gate operations, is one of the most widely used quantum simulation algorithms. However, such Trotterized implementations generally fail to preserve the symmetries of the target Hamiltonian during compilation. As a result, they can drive quantum states out of symmetrically allowed subspaces, leading to unphysical dynamics and symmetry-violating algorithmic errors. In this work, we propose a symmetry-based Trotter error mitigation protocol using classical post-processing. By applying symmetry transformations to the initial state or interleaving them between discrete Trotter layers, and then averaging an ensemble of the resulting measurement outcomes via classical post-processing, our method systematically projects out the symmetry-violating components of the Trotter error while leaving the ideal dynamics unchanged. Importantly, this framework naturally accommodates non-local spatial symmetries and anti-unitary operations such as time reversal, which are difficult or impossible to implement directly with hardware-native quantum gates. We benchmark our protocol on the one-dimensional XY model and the one-dimensional Schwinger model. In the XY model, enforcing reflection symmetry suppresses the leading-order Trotter error, whereas in the Schwinger model, interleaving gauge transformations between Trotter layers enables gauge-twirling effectively to reduce unphysical violations of local Gauss's law. These results demonstrate that symmetry-based post-processing provides a depth-preserving route to substantially improving the fidelity of Trotterized quantum simulations on near-term devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a symmetry-based Trotter error mitigation protocol using classical post-processing that projects out symmetry-violating components in quantum simulations, demonstrated on the XY model (reflection symmetry) and Schwinger model (gauge symmetry), showing significant fidelity improvements without increasing circuit depth.
AI.motivation: Standard Trotterization fails to preserve the symmetries of target Hamiltonians during compilation, causing quantum states to drift out of symmetrically allowed subspaces and producing unphysical dynamics and symmetry-violating algorithmic errors.
AI.method: Apply symmetry transformations to the initial state or interleave them between discrete Trotter layers, then average measurement outcomes via classical post-processing to systematically project out symmetry-violating components of the Trotter error while preserving ideal dynamics.
AI.result: In the XY model, enforcing reflection symmetry suppresses the leading-order Trotter error. In the Schwinger model, interleaving gauge transformations enables gauge-twirling to effectively reduce violations of local Gauss's law.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-based post-processing provides a depth-preserving route to substantially improving the fidelity of Trotterized quantum simulations on near-term devices.

title: Vine Codes: Low-Overhead Quantum LDPC Codes on a Planar Square Grid
comment: 26 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables; supplementary data available on Zenodo
summary: The surface code is a promising route towards large-scale quantum computing, requiring only nearest-neighbour gates amenable to superconducting hardware. However, surface codes incur large qubit overheads. Novel quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes promise to reduce overheads but require long-range connections that are difficult to achieve on superconducting platforms. Here, we introduce "Vine Codes" - qLDPC codes that are implementable on a planar square grid through nearest-neighbour, two-qubit gates native to superconducting platforms (iSWAP and CZ). Our approach generalises "Directional Codes" recently introduced by Gehér et. al. (2025) which are constrained to a torus. In contrast, vine codes have open boundary conditions constructed with the aid of routing qubits. We perform extensive numeric searches and find promising candidate vine codes, e.g. [[121,4,6]], [[221,6,7]], and [[234,9,6]] codes. We verify the circuit distances and show that data and measure qubits required can be reduced by up to ~28% relative to the surface code at a circuit distance of 7. Even including routing qubits, vine codes require fewer total qubits than the surface code (e.g. ~18% reduction at circuit distance 10) and benefits are expected to increase at higher distances. We perform circuit-level noise simulations to demonstrate that under a realistic noise model and at a near-term noise rate of $10^{-3}$, vine codes can perform better than the surface code while using fewer qubits. We give an exhaustive list of all unique vine codes up to stabiliser-weight 9. We additionally introduce "Flip-Vine Codes" which possess single-qubit transversal Clifford gates useful for fault-tolerant logic and magic state cultivation. We furthermore construct examples of generalised open boundaries for vine codes that go beyond the familiar X/Z boundaries of the surface and tile codes.

AI.tldr: Vine Codes are qLDPC codes implementable on planar square grids with nearest-neighbour gates, reducing qubit overhead by up to ~28% compared to surface codes while maintaining better or comparable performance under realistic noise.
AI.motivation: Surface codes require large qubit overheads, while existing qLDPC codes reduce overhead but need long-range connections unsuitable for superconducting platforms. The goal is to design qLDPC codes that combine low overhead with hardware-native nearest-neighbour connectivity on planar square grids.
AI.method: Generalise Directional Codes (Gehér et al., 2025) from torus constraints to open boundary conditions on planar square grids using routing qubits. Perform numeric searches for optimal codes up to stabiliser-weight 9, verify circuit distances, and simulate circuit-level noise at 10^{-3} error rate. Also introduce Flip-Vine Codes for transversal Clifford gates and generalised open boundaries.
AI.result: Demonstrated promising codes (e.g., [[121,4,6]], [[221,6,7]], [[234,9,6]]) with up to ~28% reduction in data and measure qubits at circuit distance 7, ~18% total qubit reduction at circuit distance 10, and better performance under near-term noise models compared to surface codes.
AI.conclusion: Vine Codes offer a practical, low-overhead alternative to surface codes for superconducting platforms, with increasing advantages at higher distances and additional benefits from transversal gates and flexible boundary conditions.

title: Extracting the physical content of Liouvillian eigenmodes: Semiclassical quantization
summary: Unlike in closed quantum systems where individual energy eigenstates are understood as physical excitations, open quantum systems have distinct right and left eigenstates of the Liouvillian that decay with time and are difficult to interpret. Here we introduce a physically motivated quasiprobability measure combining the two types of eigenstates that interprets a Liouville eigenmode as a set of coherences. This coherence measure is intimately connected to the return probability and allows one to visualize the modes as quasiprobability distributions in a "doubled" phase space. Using this measure we show that, remarkably, an oscillator retains its quantized "orbits" in phase space for a large class of linear and nonlinear damping, thus providing a formulation of semiclassical quantization for open systems. The orbits have measurable dynamical signatures and are broadened in the presence of a thermal bath, similar to energy levels. For quadratic systems, our results yield an extension of the concept of invariant tori, which play a central role in Hamiltonian systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quasiprobability measure for open quantum systems that interprets Liouvillian eigenmodes as coherences, revealing quantized phase-space orbits under damping and extending the concept of invariant tori to open systems.
AI.motivation: In open quantum systems, the right and left eigenstates of the Liouvillian decay with time and are difficult to interpret physically, unlike the clear physical meaning of energy eigenstates in closed systems.
AI.method: The authors propose a physically motivated quasiprobability measure that combines right and left eigenstates to interpret Liouville eigenmodes as coherences, linked to return probability, visualized as quasiprobability distributions in a "doubled" phase space.
AI.result: An oscillator retains quantized phase-space "orbits" for a large class of linear and nonlinear damping; these orbits have measurable dynamical signatures and become broadened in a thermal bath. For quadratic systems, the concept of invariant tori is extended to open systems.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a formulation of semiclassical quantization for open quantum systems, showing that quantized orbits persist under damping and can be measured, analogous to energy level broadening in closed systems.

title: Proposal of quantum arrival-time measurement with a Bose-Einstein condensate
summary: This work shows how a Bose-Einstein condensate of ultracold atoms could be used to address a long-standing question in quantum theory: how much time does it take for a particle to reach a detector? To this end, we propose a realistic experimental setup, whose key idea is not to measure arrival times directly, but the arrival flux on the detector as a function of its position. This novel approach not only solves practical issues with having a detector close to the system, but also results in signals that allow to unambiguously distinguish different theoretical predictions. This proposal raises prospects for resolving the decades-old debate on this fundamental issue.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using a Bose-Einstein condensate to experimentally measure quantum arrival times by detecting arrival flux as a function of detector position, offering a way to resolve the long-standing quantum time-of-arrival problem.
AI.motivation: To resolve the decades-old debate on how much time a quantum particle takes to reach a detector, a fundamental question in quantum theory that has lacked experimental resolution.
AI.method: A realistic experimental setup using a Bose-Einstein condensate of ultracold atoms where arrival times are not measured directly, but rather the arrival flux on the detector is measured as a function of its position.
AI.result: This approach solves practical issues with having a detector close to the system and yields signals that can unambiguously distinguish between different theoretical predictions for quantum arrival times.
AI.conclusion: The proposal raises prospects for experimentally resolving the fundamental and long-standing debate on quantum time of arrival.

title: Quantum Batteries as Work Sources for Phase-Locked Parametric Amplification
summary: Quantum batteries have been proposed as locally precharged work sources for superconducting quantum technologies, suggesting a route to reduce continuously supplied microwave drives. Here we ask whether the pump tone of a quantum-limited parametric amplifier can be replaced, or strongly duty-cycled, by a finite bosonic quantum battery. Quantizing the pump of a nondegenerate parametric amplifier exposes a resource distinction hidden in the classical description: stored pump energy can generate signal-idler photons, but pump phase coherence is required to generate a phase-locked amplifier field. In a closed trilinear model, coherent and phase-randomized coherent pumps with the same photon-number distribution produce comparable pair numbers, yet only the coherent pump produces anomalous two-mode coherence and an EPR-squeezed interference dip. Including leakage, we collect the emitted fields into cascaded temporal modes. At matched collector bandwidth, the coherent pump gives \(I_{\min}^{(f)}=0.553\), whereas the phase-randomized pump gives \(I_{\min}^{(f)}=1.94\) at nearly identical collected energy. Weak amplitude squeezing slightly improves the dip by reducing finite-pump number fluctuations while preserving the coherent displacement. Thus battery-powered parametric amplification requires phase-coherent stored energy, possibly assisted by number-noise reduction, rather than stored energy alone.

AI.tldr: A quantum battery can replace a classical microwave pump for parametric amplification, but only if it stores phase-coherent energy (not just energy alone). Phase-randomized pumps fail to produce EPR squeezing despite generating similar photon pairs.
AI.motivation: To explore whether the classical pump tone of a quantum-limited parametric amplifier can be replaced or duty-cycled by a finite bosonic quantum battery, potentially reducing the need for continuously supplied microwave drives in superconducting quantum technologies.
AI.method: Closed trilinear Hamiltonian model comparing coherent vs. phase-randomized coherent pumps with identical photon-number distributions; cascaded temporal mode collection with leakage; analytic calculation of minimum two-mode intensity correlation \(I_{\min}^{(f)}\) and EPR-squeezed interference dip.
AI.result: Coherent pump achieves \(I_{\min}^{(f)}=0.553\) (sub-shot-noise) while phase-randomized pump gives \(I_{\min}^{(f)}=1.94\) at nearly identical collected energy. Weak amplitude squeezing improves the dip by reducing number fluctuations while preserving coherence.
AI.conclusion: Battery-powered parametric amplification requires phase-coherent stored energy, possibly assisted by number-noise reduction, rather than stored energy alone. The quantum battery must provide phase coherence, not just population.

title: Entanglement structure of the dynamical phases in the sub-Ohmic spin-boson model
summary: The sub-Ohmic spin-boson model exhibits three distinct dynamical regimes in its spin population dynamics, classified as coherent, incoherent, and pseudo-coherent. Whether these regimes correspond to distinct spin-bath entanglement structures remains an open question. Here we address this using tree tensor network states with projector-splitting time evolution (TTN-TDVP-PS), scanning a broad grid in the sub-Ohmic $(s, α)$ plane. We find that the spin entanglement entropy $S_\mathrm{spin}(t)$ reaches a stationary plateau on a timescale shorter than the polarization relaxation, enabling construction of a stationary entropy landscape from the stationary value $S_\mathrm{stable}$. Within this scalar entropy landscape, the entropy ridge broadly follows the population-based phase boundary at small $s$, but does not reproduce the two-branch structure at large $s$. The ridge remains single-valued within the incoherent region rather than separately tracking both population-based transitions. The Bloch-sphere representation provides a geometric interpretation of this behavior. The entropy plateau corresponds to trajectories settling onto constant-radius shells, with the ridge marking the parameters of smallest stationary Bloch radius. Mode-resolved bath entanglement shows that low-frequency modes dominate the environmental entropy scale and that coherent dynamics enhance bath-mode correlations beyond direct spin--mode correlations. These results establish the stationary spin entanglement entropy as a physically informative observable that complements population-based classifications of dissipative quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: Using TTN-TDVP-PS simulations, the study maps spin-bath entanglement in the sub-Ohmic spin-boson model, finding that stationary spin entanglement entropy forms a single ridge that follows the population-based phase boundary at small s but not at large s, with low-frequency modes dominating environmental entanglement.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the three dynamical regimes (coherent, incoherent, pseudo-coherent) in the sub-Ohmic spin-boson model correspond to distinct spin-bath entanglement structures—a question that remained open.
AI.method: Tree tensor network states with projector-splitting time evolution (TTN-TDVP-PS) across a broad grid in the sub-Ohmic (s, α) plane; analysis of spin entanglement entropy, Bloch-sphere representation, and mode-resolved bath entanglement.
AI.result: Stationary spin entanglement entropy forms a single-valued ridge that aligns with the population-based phase boundary at small s but does not reproduce the two-branch structure at large s. Low-frequency bath modes dominate environmental entanglement, and coherent dynamics enhance bath-mode correlations beyond direct spin-mode correlations.
AI.conclusion: Stationary spin entanglement entropy is a physically informative observable that complements population-based classifications of dissipative quantum dynamics.

title: Exploiting More Than Symmetry in Variational Quantum Machine Learning
summary: The success of variational quantum learning models crucially depends on choosing parametrizations that reflect the structure of the problem at hand. Symmetries provide one of the clearest such structures: whenever transformations of the input leave the desired outcome unchanged, this invariance should be built into the model rather than discovered during training. However, imposing a symmetry does not by itself determine a useful ansatz. Even within the symmetry-preserving space, one must decide where the trainable degrees of freedom should be placed. In this work, we study this remaining design freedom in equivariant variational quantum circuits. Building on symmetry-based parameter sharing, we disentangle two architectural choices: how much symmetry should be enforced, and which symmetry-respecting interactions should be trainable. Using Tic-Tac-Toe as a fully enumerable and structurally transparent test case, we find that suitable subgroups preserve most of the generalization benefit. By contrast, the dominant gains arise from gates acting directly on decisive task motifs. Thus, symmetry defines the admissible design space, while effective ansatze require an additional task-informed choice of trainable interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to design equivariant variational quantum circuits by disentangling symmetry enforcement from the choice of trainable interactions, showing that while symmetry defines the admissible design space, effective ansätze require task-informed decisions about which gates to train.
AI.motivation: The success of variational quantum learning models depends on choosing parametrizations that reflect problem structure. Symmetries provide clear structure, but imposing a symmetry does not by itself determine a useful ansatz—one must still decide where trainable degrees of freedom should be placed within the symmetry-preserving space.
AI.method: The study disentangles two architectural choices in equivariant variational quantum circuits: (1) how much symmetry should be enforced, and (2) which symmetry-respecting interactions should be trainable. Using Tic-Tac-Toe as a fully enumerable and structurally transparent test case, the authors systematically explore these design dimensions.
AI.result: Suitable subgroups preserve most of the generalization benefit of full symmetry enforcement. However, the dominant gains arise not from symmetry alone but from gates acting directly on decisive task motifs—the task-informed choice of trainable interactions is the primary driver of performance.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry defines the admissible design space for equivariant quantum circuits, but effective ansätze require an additional task-informed choice of which interactions to make trainable. This separates the roles of symmetry (constraining the space) and task-motivated gate placement (driving performance gains).

title: Effective Faraday interaction between light and Helium-3 nuclear spins in a multi-pass cell
summary: Helium-3 nuclear spins form an exceptionally stable quantum system with extremely long coherence time, offering exciting opportunities for quantum technologies. In particular, nuclear spin-squeezed states promise enhanced precision for sensing tasks and tests of new physics. A central challenge for all these applications is the realization of a controllable light-nuclear spin interface. Here we experimentally demonstrate such an interface by exploiting metastability-exchange collisions in a low-pressure helium-3 gas cell at room temperature. A radio-frequency discharge produces a small population of metastable atoms that both enables efficient optical pumping and mediates an effective Faraday interaction between the collective nuclear spin and an optical probe. We quantitatively characterize the strength of this interaction as a function of the nuclear polarization, applied magnetic field, and probe-beam parameters. Moreover, we show that using a multi-pass cell enhances this interaction by effectively increasing the optical depth. Extrapolating to a tenfold increase of the probe power used in the present experiment, we project a measurement-induced squeezing rate of 0.52 s$^{-1}$. Our results provide a practical pathway for optical access to helium-3 nuclear spins and open prospects for generating long-lived, macroscopic nuclear spin-squeezed states for quantum metrology.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates a controllable light-nuclear spin interface in a helium-3 gas cell using metastability-exchange collisions, enabling efficient optical pumping and Faraday interaction for nuclear spin squeezing. Using a multi-pass cell enhances interaction, with a projected squeezing rate of 0.52 s⁻¹ at higher probe power.
AI.motivation: Helium-3 nuclear spins have exceptionally long coherence times beneficial for quantum technologies and sensing, but a controllable light-nuclear spin interface is needed for applications like spin-squeezed states.
AI.method: Metastability-exchange collisions in a low-pressure helium-3 gas cell at room temperature with RF discharge, optical pumping, Faraday interaction, and multi-pass cell enhancement.
AI.result: Quantitative characterization of interaction strength versus nuclear polarization, magnetic field, and probe parameters; multi-pass cell enhances optical depth; projected squeezing rate of 0.52 s⁻¹ with tenfold increased probe power.
AI.conclusion: This provides a practical pathway for optical access to helium-3 nuclear spins and opens prospects for generating long-lived macroscopic nuclear spin-squeezed states for quantum metrology.

title: Observation of alignment tensor effects in metastability-exchange collisions with highly polarized 3He ensembles
summary: Highly polarized 3He ensembles prepared by metastability-exchange optical pumping (MEOP) have been widely used in precision measurements and fundamental physics. Metastability-exchange (ME) collisions, serving as the basis of MEOP, are traditionally described in terms of atomic orientation, while the significant contributions of metastable alignment tensor at high polarization remain unexplored. In this work, we develop a linearized model under mean-field approximation to investigate alignment tensor effects in highly polarized 3He , which originate from the metastable F = 3/2 manifold and are revealed through ME-induced relaxation and frequency shift. By means of free-induction-decay (FID) measurements, a pronounced dependence on nuclear polarization is experimentally observed in the response of the ground-state-metastable hybrid 3He ensembles to the external magnetic field. Furthermore, after obtaining the characteristics of tensor-induced phenomena, we demonstrate good agreement between the experiment and the theory. This work advances the understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized 3He using MEOP. It further provides applications in systematic error correction of high-accuracy magnetometry, as well as in optimal protocol for the generation of nuclear spin-squeezed states.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a linearized model to study alignment tensor effects in highly polarized 3He ensembles prepared by metastability-exchange optical pumping (MEOP), experimentally observes tensor-induced relaxation and frequency shifts via free-induction-decay measurements, and achieves good theory-experiment agreement, advancing understanding of nuclear spin dynamics and enabling applications in high-accuracy magnetometry and spin-squeezed state generation.
AI.motivation: Metastability-exchange collisions in MEOP have traditionally been described using atomic orientation, but the significant contributions of the metastable alignment tensor at high polarization were unexplored, motivating the need to investigate these effects.
AI.method: A linearized model under mean-field approximation was developed to analyze alignment tensor effects originating from the metastable F = 3/2 manifold. Free-induction-decay (FID) measurements were performed on ground-state-metastable hybrid 3He ensembles to experimentally observe the nuclear polarization dependence.
AI.result: A pronounced dependence on nuclear polarization was experimentally observed in the response of hybrid 3He ensembles to external magnetic fields. After characterizing the tensor-induced phenomena, good agreement between experiment and theory was demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: The work advances the understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized 3He using MEOP and provides applications for systematic error correction in high-accuracy magnetometry and optimal protocols for generating nuclear spin-squeezed states.

title: Phase locking nuclear spins in silicon with spin-orbit coupling
summary: Because they have such long coherence times, nuclear spins have extraordinary potential for use in quantum information processing devices. However, coherent nuclear spin control generally requires external phase references, such as microwave control fields. Here, we phase-lock a $^{29}$Si nuclear spin ensemble in a silicon quantum dot using only the internal electronic spin-orbit coupling as a phase reference. When driven with the quantum-dot electrons, the nuclear spins align themselves to a phase determined by the electronic spin-orbit coupling and the timing of the drive protocol. This enables us to measure the coherent precession and inhomogeneous dephasing of the nuclear spins. We corroborate our results with detailed numerical simulations of the many-body electron nuclear system. Our work opens new routes for coherently controlling solid-state nuclear spin ensembles.

AI.tldr: Nuclear spins in a silicon quantum dot are phase-locked using only internal electronic spin-orbit coupling, enabling coherent precession measurement and dephasing characterization without external phase references.
AI.motivation: Nuclear spins have long coherence times ideal for quantum information processing, but their coherent control typically requires external phase references like microwave fields; this work aims to eliminate that requirement.
AI.method: A $^{29}$Si nuclear spin ensemble in a silicon quantum dot is phase-locked via internal electronic spin-orbit coupling. The nuclear spins align to a phase determined by the spin-orbit coupling and drive protocol timing, using only quantum-dot electrons as a driving mechanism.
AI.result: Successful phase-locking of the nuclear spin ensemble enables measurement of coherent precession and inhomogeneous dephasing of the nuclear spins. Results are corroborated by detailed many-body numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: This work opens new routes for coherently controlling solid-state nuclear spin ensembles without external phase references, leveraging internal spin-orbit coupling for phase synchronization.

title: Quantum ring all-reduce: communication and privacy advantages for distributed learning
summary: Machine learning models have scaled to unprecedented sizes, making training across distributed devices the de facto standard in the field. In this work, we explore how quantum communications can make distributed training both more communication-efficient and information-theoretically private, for both classical and quantum learning models. Ring all-reduce is the foundational communication primitive for large-scale distributed training. We present a quantum version that reduces per-link online communication by a provably optimal factor of two using pre-shared entanglement and superdense coding, without requiring the learning model or gradient computation to change. Beyond bandwidth, the primitive enables privacy guarantees that are information-theoretically impossible for any classical protocol, achieving composable ε-secure aggregation, via verified entanglement, at a 2x overhead in GHZ copies. Our hybrid quantum-classical communication architecture yields simultaneous communication and security advantages for large scale distributed training, regardless of whether the learning itself is quantum or classical. Finally, we characterise quantum advantages in gradient conflict detection for server-to-client communication under bandwidth constraints, a setting that arises after ring all-reduce is completed, when full gradient broadcast to external clients is infeasible. Two variants of the problem admit different separations. For margin-based alignment testing (\textsc{GapIP}_τ), the quantum advantage is quadratic in the margin parameter: \widetilde{O}(τ^{-1}\log P) qubits versus \widetilde{O}(\min(\τ^{-2},P)) bits. For sign-consistency auditing against a private parameter matching (\textsc{TieAudit}_ε), the advantage represents an exponential separation in communication complexity: Ω(\sqrt{P}) bits whereas O(ε^{-2}\log P) qubits suffice.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum communication primitive based on ring all-reduce that uses pre-shared entanglement and superdense coding to halve per-link communication, provides information-theoretic privacy guarantees (ε-secure aggregation) unattainable by classical protocols, and demonstrates quadratic to exponential quantum advantages in gradient conflict detection tasks for server-client communication under bandwidth constraints.
AI.motivation: Large-scale distributed training of machine learning models faces fundamental bottlenecks in communication efficiency and privacy. Classical communication protocols incur high bandwidth costs and cannot achieve information-theoretic security. This work explores whether quantum communications can simultaneously address both challenges for distributed training of classical and quantum models.
AI.method: The authors propose a quantum version of the ring all-reduce primitive using pre-shared entanglement and superdense coding to double the effective bandwidth. They incorporate verified entanglement (GHZ states) to achieve composable ε-secure aggregation with only 2x overhead in GHZ copies. For gradient conflict detection, they analyze two variants: margin-based alignment testing (GapIP_τ) and sign-consistency auditing (TieAudit_ε), providing quantum communication protocols with provable advantages.
AI.result: The quantum ring all-reduce achieves a provably optimal factor-of-two reduction in per-link online communication. The privacy guarantees are information-theoretically impossible for any classical protocol. For GapIP_τ, the quantum advantage is quadratic in the margin parameter: Õ(τ^{-1} log P) qubits vs Õ(min(τ^{-2}, P)) bits. For TieAudit_ε, an exponential separation emerges: Ω(√P) bits vs O(ε^{-2} log P) qubits.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical communication architectures provide simultaneous communication efficiency and security advantages for large-scale distributed training, applicable whether the learning model itself is quantum or classical. The results demonstrate fundamental quantum advantages in both the all-reduce primitive and downstream gradient conflict detection tasks.

title: Effective discrete-modulated continuous variable QKD under general attacks
summary: Continuous variable quantum key distribution via discrete modulations ensures information-theoretic security using standard telecom technologies, providing affordable and scalable quantum communications with simplified classical postprocessing. However, existing security proofs against general attacks often rely on restrictive assumptions, such as a bounded dimension for coherent states, or require impractically large block sizes. In this work, we develop a finite-size security analysis that removes these limitations while incorporating realistic experimental features. Our approach combines the dimension reduction technique, a security proof based on the marginal-constrained entropy accumulation, and a trusted detector model accounting for the receiver imperfections. We report positive key rates in the finite-size regime for relevant block sizes of the order of $10^8$. These results contribute to narrowing the gap between theoretical security proofs and practical implementations of discrete-modulated continuous variable quantum key distribution protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a finite-size security analysis for discrete-modulated continuous variable QKD that removes restrictive assumptions (bounded dimension, large block sizes) while incorporating realistic experimental features, achieving positive key rates for block sizes of ~10^8.
AI.motivation: Existing security proofs for discrete-modulated CV-QKD rely on restrictive assumptions (e.g., bounded coherent state dimension) or require impractically large block sizes, creating a gap between theoretical security and practical implementations.
AI.method: The approach combines dimension reduction technique, security proof based on marginal-constrained entropy accumulation, and a trusted detector model accounting for receiver imperfections.
AI.result: Positive key rates are achieved in the finite-size regime for relevant block sizes of ~10^8.
AI.conclusion: This work narrows the gap between theoretical security proofs and practical implementations of discrete-modulated CV-QKD protocols.

title: Discrimination of genuinely nonlocal sets without entanglement in multipartite systems
summary: Genuine nonlocality arises when a set of multipartite orthogonal states is locally indistinguishable under any bipartition of the subsystems. The entanglement-assisted discrimination of such genuinely nonlocal orthogonal product sets has attracted significant attention in quantum information. Based on the criterion of local irreducibility, genuine nonlocality is classified into Type I (reducible) and Type II (irreducible). We present entanglement-assisted discrimination schemes for both types of genuinely nonlocal sets that use minimal resources. For low-dimensional cases, Type I sets require only a single EPR pair, whereas Type II sets necessitate only one GHZ state. We extend these protocols to higher-dimensional systems: the discrimination of Type I sets requires only one maximally entangled state in a two-qutrit system, while that of Type II sets similarly demands a single maximally entangled state in a three-qutrit system. For $n$-partite ($n > 3$) systems, Type I sets continue to require only one maximally entangled state, whereas Type II sets necessitate just one additional EPR pair compared to their Type I counterparts. These results provide a robust framework for the efficient discrimination of genuinely nonlocal sets using minimal quantum resources.

AI.tldr: This paper presents entanglement-assisted discrimination schemes for two types of genuine nonlocality (Type I and Type II) that use minimal quantum resources: Type I sets require only a single EPR pair (or one maximally entangled state in higher dimensions), while Type II sets need one GHZ state (or one additional EPR pair for n>3 systems), providing an efficient framework for discriminating genuinely nonlocal orthogonal product sets.
AI.motivation: To develop resource-efficient entanglement-assisted discrimination protocols for genuinely nonlocal orthogonal product sets, addressing the open problem of minimizing quantum resources needed to distinguish these sets that are locally indistinguishable under any bipartition.
AI.method: Based on the criterion of local irreducibility, the authors classify genuine nonlocality into Type I (reducible) and Type II (irreducible). They design entanglement-assisted discrimination schemes using minimal resources: EPR pairs for Type I sets and GHZ states for Type II sets, then generalize these protocols to higher-dimensional and multipartite systems.
AI.result: Type I sets require only a single EPR pair (low-dim) or one maximally entangled state (higher-dim). Type II sets need only one GHZ state (low-dim) or one maximally entangled state in three-qutrit systems. For n-partite (n>3) systems, Type I needs one maximally entangled state; Type II needs just one additional EPR pair over Type I.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a robust framework for efficiently discriminating genuinely nonlocal sets using minimal quantum resources, offering optimized resource consumption for both types of genuine nonlocality across various dimensions and multipartite configurations.

title: Sparse Configuration Interaction for the Electronic Schrödinger Equation Revisited: Complete Basis Set Limit Complexity and Quantum-Encoding Impact
summary: In this article we revisit regularity results for eigenfunctions in the discrete spectrum of the electronic Schrödinger equation and study their consequences for approximation complexity. In particular, for the convergence to the complete basis set limit, it can be shown that the curse of dimensionality in the leading algebraic exponent can be mitigated. That is, for general sparse grid constructions, the main term of the convergence rate with respect to the number of degrees of freedom is independent of the number of electrons. These insights indicate potential benefits for classical numerical solvers of the electronic Schrödinger equation and also for quantum-computing approaches through new qubit-efficient wavefunction encodings.
