AI.tldr: This paper revisits regularity results for eigenfunctions of the electronic Schrödinger equation and shows that the curse of dimensionality in approximation complexity can be mitigated for discrete spectrum eigenfunctions, leading to convergence rates independent of electron number for sparse grid constructions, with implications for both classical and quantum computing methods.
AI.motivation: To revisit regularity results for eigenfunctions in the discrete spectrum of the electronic Schrödinger equation and study their consequences for approximation complexity, particularly addressing the curse of dimensionality.
AI.method: Analyzes regularity of eigenfunctions in the discrete spectrum of the electronic Schrödinger equation and derives convergence rates for sparse grid constructions in the complete basis set limit.
AI.result: The curse of dimensionality in the leading algebraic exponent can be mitigated: the main term of the convergence rate with respect to the number of degrees of freedom is independent of the number of electrons for general sparse grid constructions.
AI.conclusion: These insights indicate potential benefits for classical numerical solvers and quantum-computing approaches through new qubit-efficient wavefunction encodings.

title: Interaction geometry and ground-state properties of sparse quantum lattice models
summary: We investigate how interaction geometry shapes the low-energy phases of sparse tunable long-range quantum models. We focus on a class of graphs whose degree grows logarithmically with system size, and show how symmetry and frustration in graph connectivity can drive, suppress, and reshape ground-state phase transitions. The central examples are power-of-$p$ graphs, where even and odd values of $p$ exhibit qualitatively distinct behaviour: even-$p$ graphs inherit the rich phase structure of the power-of-two model, while odd-$p$ graphs are governed by geometric frustration. Fibonacci graphs provide a contrasting case, lacking the discrete self-similarity of the power-of-$p$ family but exhibiting a direct geometric mapping between the short- and long-range limits. Across our models, we find that phase structure and criticality are governed by the same effective-geometry principle, unifying our framework for experimentally motivated long-range quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how interaction geometry (graph connectivity) influences low-energy phases of sparse, tunable long-range quantum models. Power-of-p graphs show distinct behavior based on parity (even vs. odd), with even-p mirroring power-of-two phases and odd-p dominated by geometric frustration. Fibonacci graphs lack discrete self-similarity but map directly between short- and long-range limits. A unified effective-geometry principle governs phase structure and criticality across all models.
AI.motivation: To understand how graph connectivity, symmetry, and frustration shape ground-state phase transitions in sparse long-range quantum systems, motivated by experimentally realizable quantum models (e.g., trapped ions, Rydberg arrays) where interaction geometry is tunable.
AI.method: The authors analyze a class of graphs with logarithmically growing degree, focusing on power-of-p graphs (where parity controls phase behavior) and Fibonacci graphs (which lack discrete self-similarity). They compare phase structures and criticality across these graph families, identifying an effective-geometry principle that unifies the observed behavior.
AI.result: Even-p power-of-p graphs inherit the rich phase structure of the power-of-two model, while odd-p graphs are governed by geometric frustration. Fibonacci graphs exhibit a direct geometric mapping between short- and long-range limits despite lacking discrete self-similarity. Phase structure and criticality across all models are governed by the same effective-geometry principle.
AI.conclusion: Interaction geometry fundamentally determines low-energy phases in sparse long-range quantum models. The effective-geometry principle provides a unifying framework that connects symmetry, frustration, and phase transitions across different graph families, offering insights for experimentally motivated tunable quantum systems.

title: Faking entanglement with imperceptible measurement deviations
summary: Quantum entanglement is a central resource underpinning emerging quantum technologies, enabling capabilities beyond those of classical systems. Accurate verification of entanglement is therefore crucial. However, experimental schemes usually rely on the assumption that quantum measurements can be realized exactly. As the complexity of a quantum system grows, this assumption typically becomes increasingly unrealistic, therefore leading to a widening mismatch between theoretical models and experimental implementations. Here we demonstrate that arbitrarily small measurement errors, when adversarially encoded in the measurement apparatus, can lead to the false certification of high-dimensional entanglement in systems that are, in fact, separable. This is achieved by introducing explicit hacking attacks to measurement devices in well-established entanglement verification tests. We further experimentally demonstrate this effect using classical photonic states encoded in the spatial degree of freedom, spanning up to 61 dimensions with measurement fidelity errors as low as 0.23%. Our results uncover a fundamental vulnerability in current methods for high-dimensional entanglement detection, highlighting the susceptibility of complex quantum devices to small adversarial perturbations. The findings underscore the need for developing secure verification of quantum information that is robust to bounded discrepancies between theory and experiment.

AI.tldr: Small measurement errors can falsely certify high-dimensional entanglement in separable systems, demonstrated theoretically and experimentally with up to 61-dimensional photonic states and 0.23% measurement fidelity errors.
AI.motivation: Accurate entanglement verification is crucial for quantum technologies, but experimental schemes assume exact quantum measurements, which becomes unrealistic in complex systems, leading to a gap between theory and experiment.
AI.method: The authors introduce adversarial hacking attacks on measurement devices in standard entanglement verification tests, and experimentally demonstrate false certification using classical photonic states encoded in spatial degrees of freedom up to 61 dimensions with measurement fidelity errors as low as 0.23%.
AI.result: Arbitrarily small measurement errors can falsely certify high-dimensional entanglement in separable systems; experimentally demonstrated up to 61 dimensions with 0.23% fidelity errors.
AI.conclusion: Current high-dimensional entanglement detection methods are fundamentally vulnerable to small adversarial perturbations, highlighting the need for robust verification methods that tolerate bounded theory-experiment discrepancies.

title: Quantum Kernels are Spectral Tensor Networks
summary: Quantum kernels admit Fourier representations whose frequencies are determined by the data-encoding gates of the underlying feature map. We show that entangling tensor kernels are matrix product operator factorizations of the corresponding Fourier coefficient tensors, thereby identifying quantum kernels as spectral tensor networks. By grouping gate-level frequency configurations that yield the same feature-wise frequency, we obtain a grouped Fourier form that induces a more compact spectral tensor network representation of the kernel. We further show that kernel target alignment serves as a bridge between the Fourier and tensor network views. On a grid that resolves the accessible Fourier modes, it becomes the Frobenius cosine similarity between Fourier coefficient tensors. Our numerical experiments show that layered quantum kernels admit accurate representations with small bond dimension, revealing a compressibility governed by correlations between Fourier modes. This compressibility provides a diagnostic of classical representability and of whether kernel evaluation is likely to remain classically tractable.

AI.tldr: Quantum kernels can be represented as spectral tensor networks via Fourier analysis, with compressibility determined by Fourier mode correlations, offering a diagnostic for classical tractability.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between quantum kernel methods and tensor network representations, enabling analysis of classical representability and tractability of quantum kernel evaluation.
AI.method: The authors show entangling tensor kernels are matrix product operator factorizations of Fourier coefficient tensors, derive a grouped Fourier form for compact spectral tensor network representation, and connect kernel target alignment to Frobenius cosine similarity between Fourier coefficient tensors.
AI.result: Layered quantum kernels admit accurate representations with small bond dimension, indicating compressibility governed by correlations between Fourier modes.
AI.conclusion: Compressibility of the spectral tensor network provides a diagnostic for classical representability and whether kernel evaluation remains classically tractable.

title: Computing noise-canceling observables via Pauli propagation
summary: The pursuit of quantum advantage is driving the co-evolution of quantum processors and classical simulation methods. Despite advances in scale and quality, the accuracy of quantum simulation is ultimately limited by error rates and sampling overheads. Similarly, while classical simulation methods such as Pauli propagation have made remarkable progress, their accuracy is ultimately limited by the exponential growth of operator paths and the truncations needed to control memory and runtime. Here we show that these complementary limitations can be mitigated by embedding Pauli propagation within a hybrid error-mitigation framework that reduces quantum sampling overhead while achieving lower truncation errors with fewer classical resources than traditional Pauli propagation alone. In this framework, a target observable is classically propagated through noise-canceling inverse channels, producing a modified observable that is measured directly on a quantum processor. We prototype two implementations and benchmark their performance numerically on canonical models that challenge traditional Pauli propagation. We also perform experiments on a quantum processor using 56 superconducting qubits, revealing the tradeoffs of their respective truncation strategies. These results illustrate how classical and quantum resources can be orchestrated to extend observable estimation beyond the limits of either approach alone, providing a foundation for quantum-centric supercomputing and future demonstrations of quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid classical-quantum framework that embeds Pauli propagation within error mitigation, enabling more accurate observable estimation beyond what classical or quantum methods can achieve alone, demonstrated numerically and on a 56-qubit superconducting processor.
AI.motivation: Both quantum simulation (limited by error rates and sampling overhead) and classical Pauli propagation (limited by exponential operator path growth and truncation) face fundamental accuracy barriers. The goal is to overcome these complementary limitations by orchestrating classical and quantum resources synergistically.
AI.method: A target observable is classically propagated through noise-canceling inverse channels, yielding a modified observable measured directly on a quantum processor. Two prototype implementations with different truncation strategies are developed and tested.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks on canonical models show the hybrid approach achieves lower truncation errors with fewer classical resources than traditional Pauli propagation alone. Experiments on 56 superconducting qubits reveal tradeoffs between the two truncation strategies.
AI.conclusion: Classical and quantum resources can be orchestrated to extend observable estimation beyond the limits of either approach alone, providing a foundation for quantum-centric supercomputing and future quantum advantage demonstrations.

title: Many-body chirality of topological stabilizer states
summary: A defining feature of chirality is the distinction between a system and its mirror image. Despite extensive experimental observations of chiral phases and theoretical advances, a quantum-information theoretic characterization of chirality based solely on the entanglement structure of many-body quantum states remains elusive. Here, we introduce the notion of many-body chirality by formulating it as an obstruction to transforming a quantum state into its complex conjugate through finite-depth local operations. We rigorously establish many-body chirality for stabilizer realizations of $\mathbb{Z}_d^{(k)}$ anyon theories, proving that complex conjugation can be implemented by local quantum channels if and only if the underlying anyon data are mirror invariant. This reveals forms of chirality that evade conventional diagnostics, including examples with vanishing modular commutator, vanishing chiral central charge, and commuting-projector realizations. We further show that this obstruction is intrinsically four-partite, while invisible to tripartite entanglement structure. Finally, we prove that $\mathbb{Z}_d^{(k)}$ states with $d>2$ possess intrinsic many-body imaginarity: their complex phase structure cannot be removed by finite-depth local unitaries. Remarkably, this includes states that are not many-body chiral.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces many-body chirality as an obstruction to transforming a quantum state into its complex conjugate via finite-depth local operations. For ℤ_d^(k) anyon theories, complex conjugation is implementable by local quantum channels iff the anyon data are mirror invariant. This reveals chirality beyond conventional diagnostics (vanishing modular commutator, chiral central charge, commuting-projector realizations). The obstruction is intrinsically four-partite and ℤ_d^(k) states with d>2 possess intrinsic many-body imaginarity, including non-chiral states.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum-information theoretic characterization of chirality based solely on the entanglement structure of many-body quantum states, beyond conventional experimental and theoretical approaches.
AI.method: Formulating many-body chirality as an obstruction to transforming a quantum state into its complex conjugate through finite-depth local operations; analyzing stabilizer realizations of ℤ_d^(k) anyon theories using local quantum channels and entanglement measures.
AI.result: Complex conjugation is implementable by local quantum channels iff the underlying anyon data are mirror invariant. Identifies chiral states that evade conventional diagnostics (vanishing modular commutator, vanishing chiral central charge, commuting-projector realizations). The obstruction is intrinsically four-partite but invisible to tripartite entanglement. ℤ_d^(k) states with d>2 have intrinsic many-body imaginarity.
AI.conclusion: Many-body chirality is a robust entanglement-based notion that reveals new forms of chirality beyond standard measures, and intrinsic many-body imaginarity exists even in non-chiral states for d>2.

title: Fidelity bounds for adiabatic gates and other quantum operations with time-dependent dissipation
summary: As quantum-computing platforms are susceptible to noise, the fidelity of quantum operations is limited by decoherence. Understanding this limitation is crucial for building utility-scale quantum processors. In previous works [Phys. Rev. Lett. 129, 150504 (2022); Quantum 9, 1684 (2025)], we presented analytical formulae for the average gate fidelity of multi-qubit operations under static Markovian noise processes, including operations that temporarily leave the computational subspace. However, some quantum-computing architectures dynamically modulate qubit or coupler frequencies to implement two-qubit gates, e.g., baseband flux gates; such modulation can lead to dissipation rates varying in time. In this Letter, we therefore generalize the fidelity-reduction formulae to encompass time-dependent dissipation. Applying our generalized formula, we obtain a fidelity bound for adiabatic operations and demonstrate that flux-dependent noise sensitivity, combined with qubit-coupler hybridization, significantly reduces the fidelity of adiabatic controlled-Z (CZ) gates in superconducting quantum computers. Our work thus provides essential theoretical tools for evaluating error budgets and optimizing the design of quantum operations in tunable quantum-computing architectures, and may also find applications in quantum-sensing and quantum-communication protocols that are affected by time-dependent dissipation.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes fidelity-reduction formulae for multi-qubit operations under Markovian noise to include time-dependent dissipation, applies the result to bound adiabatic gate fidelity, and shows that flux-dependent noise and qubit-coupler hybridization significantly degrade adiabatic CZ gate fidelity in superconducting qubits.
AI.motivation: Understanding how decoherence limits quantum operation fidelity is crucial for building utility-scale quantum processors, but existing analytical formulae for average gate fidelity under static Markovian noise do not cover architectures (e.g., baseband flux gates) where dissipation rates vary dynamically in time.
AI.method: The authors generalize their previous analytical fidelity-reduction formulae (Phys. Rev. Lett. 129, 150504 (2022); Quantum 9, 1684 (2025)) to accommodate time-dependent dissipation rates, then apply the generalized formula to derive a fidelity bound for adiabatic operations and analyze flux-dependent noise sensitivity with qubit-coupler hybridization.
AI.result: A generalized fidelity formula for time-dependent dissipation is obtained; applying it shows that flux-dependent noise sensitivity combined with qubit-coupler hybridization significantly reduces the fidelity of adiabatic controlled-Z (CZ) gates in superconducting quantum computers.
AI.conclusion: The work provides essential theoretical tools for evaluating error budgets and optimizing quantum operation design in tunable quantum-computing architectures, with potential applications also in quantum sensing and quantum communication protocols affected by time-dependent dissipation.

title: General circuit mapping algorithm for neutral atom quantum computers
summary: Neutral atom quantum computers (NAQC) are emerging as a promising, scalable quantum computing platform because of their long qubit coherence, flexible qubit arrangement, and multiqubit gate capabilities. However, circuit execution often requires physically moving qubits, making compilation a critical optimization challenge. We propose a circuit independent mathematical framework built on graph-theoretic combinatorial optimization that determines the minimal number of required qubit transfers. This model captures spatial constraints specific to NAQC platforms with zone-limited gate operations and multi-qubit gates. From this framework, we encode the qubit mapping problem as a nonlinear integer program and solve it using a genetic algorithm, enabling trade-offs between minimizing the total traveled distance and the number of parallel transfer operations. Compared to the state-of-the-art scalable compiler for zoned architectures, our approach consistently finds fewer transfers. Depending on the optimization focus, our method produces shorter traveled distances or fewer parallel transfer operations. This work provides both theoretical guaranties and a practical tool for efficient, architecture-aware quantum circuit compilation. As a result, practitioners can generate hardware-aware mappings that reduce movement-induced errors and better exploit atom transfer parallelism, directly improving execution efficiency on NAQC devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a graph-theoretic combinatorial optimization framework for minimizing qubit transfers in neutral atom quantum computers, formulated as a nonlinear integer program solved via genetic algorithm, achieving fewer transfers, shorter distances, or fewer parallel operations compared to state-of-the-art compilers for zoned architectures.
AI.motivation: Neutral atom quantum computers require physical qubit movement during circuit execution, making compilation critical for performance. Existing compilation approaches lack rigorous optimization guarantees for minimizing qubit transfers in zone-limited architectures.
AI.method: A circuit-independent graph-theoretic combinatorial optimization framework that models spatial constraints of NAQC platforms as a nonlinear integer program, solved using a genetic algorithm to trade off total traveled distance versus parallel transfer operations.
AI.result: Compared to state-of-the-art scalable compiler for zoned architectures, the proposed method consistently finds fewer transfers, and depending on optimization focus, produces shorter traveled distances or fewer parallel transfer operations.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides both theoretical guarantees and a practical tool for architecture-aware quantum circuit compilation, enabling practitioners to generate hardware-aware mappings that reduce movement-induced errors and exploit atom transfer parallelism, directly improving execution efficiency on NAQC devices.

title: Entropy Estimation in Multi-Qutrit Systems via Variational and Classical Neural Networks
summary: We present a systematic study of von Neumann entropy estimation in multi-qutrit quantum systems using two complementary approaches: variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) and classical convolutional neural networks (CNNs), evaluated using an ideal (noise-free) quantum simulator. For systems up to three qutrits, we construct and evaluate 11 hardware-efficient SU(3)-inspired ansatzes. A parameter sweep shows that estimation accuracy is primarily determined by the number of trainable parameters, provided sufficient entanglement is present. Based on this study, we fix the parameter count to approximately 120 for subsequent experiments, observing that increasing entangling-gate counts beyond a threshold yields only marginal improvements. For larger systems (two to five qutrits), we use a CNN trained on measurement outcomes from tensor-product mutually unbiased bases. The model achieves accurate and stable predictions and exhibits a systematic improvement in performance with system size, with the highest errors for two-qutrit systems and the lowest for five-qutrit systems. Notably, using only 12.5% of the measurements required for full state tomography is sufficient to reach 90th-percentile absolute errors of approximately 0.13-0.16 nats for both four- and five-qutrit systems. The CNN model is also robust to shot noise and generalizes well to out-of-distribution states. Overall, within the simulated settings studied here, our results indicate a transition in practical methods: VQAs are effective for small systems, while CNN-based estimators offer improved scalability and robustness for larger qutrit systems.

AI.tldr: This paper compares variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) and classical convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for von Neumann entropy estimation in multi-qutrit systems using an ideal quantum simulator. VQAs work well for small systems (up to 3 qutrits), while CNNs trained on partial measurement data scale better and are more robust for larger systems (2-5 qutrits), achieving accurate predictions with only 12.5% of full tomography measurements.
AI.motivation: To systematically study and compare two complementary approaches (VQAs and CNNs) for von Neumann entropy estimation in multi-qutrit systems, and to identify which method is more suitable depending on system size.
AI.method: (1) For VQAs: constructed 11 hardware-efficient SU(3)-inspired ansatzes for up to 3 qutrits, performed parameter sweep to study accuracy vs. trainable parameters and entangling-gate count. (2) For CNNs: trained on measurement outcomes from tensor-product mutually unbiased bases, evaluated on 2-5 qutrit systems, tested robustness to shot noise and out-of-distribution states.
AI.result: VQA accuracy is primarily determined by number of trainable parameters (~120 used); increasing entangling gates beyond a threshold yields marginal gains. CNN achieves accurate, stable predictions with systematic improvement as system size increases. Using only 12.5% of full tomography measurements achieves 90th-percentile absolute errors of ~0.13-0.16 nats for 4- and 5-qutrit systems. CNN is robust to shot noise and generalizes well.
AI.conclusion: VQAs are effective for small qutrit systems, while CNN-based estimators offer improved scalability and robustness for larger qutrit systems, indicating a practical method transition depending on system size.

title: Approximating optimal decoding of quantum LDPC codes with narrow frontiers
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures Implementation available at https://github.com/aleverrier/frontier
summary:
We introduce the Frontier decoder, a pruned dynamic-programming decoder for sparse quantum decoding problems. Frontier processes error variables in a chosen order, merges prefixes with the same residual syndrome and logical label, and approximates logical-coset posterior masses by retaining only a narrow scored frontier. Without pruning, the recursion is exact ordered inference with exponential complexity.
  In the code-capacity setting, the decoder reaches thresholds close to optimal for the surface code and the color code. In the circuit-level noise model, it achieves state-of-the-art performance with a very small average retained list size: less than 100 for the gross code $[[144,12,12]]$ at a physical error rate of $0.001$. When the list size is constant, the decoder has linear complexity, suggesting the possibility of low-latency implementations.

AI.tldr: The Frontier decoder is a pruned dynamic-programming decoder for quantum error correction that achieves state-of-the-art performance (e.g., for the [[144,12,12]] gross code at p=0.001, average list size <100) with linear complexity when list size is constant, enabling potential low-latency implementations.
AI.motivation: Quantum decoding is inherently exponential in complexity when solved exactly via ordered inference; a practical decoder must prune the search space while preserving near-optimal decoding accuracy.
AI.method: Frontier processes error variables sequentially, merges prefixes sharing the same residual syndrome and logical label, and retains only a narrow scored frontier to approximate logical-coset posterior masses.
AI.result: Achieves thresholds close to optimal for surface and color codes in code-capacity setting; state-of-the-art circuit-level performance with average list size <100 for [[144,12,12]] gross code at p=0.001; linear complexity with constant list size.
AI.conclusion: The Frontier decoder demonstrates that highly pruned dynamic programming can deliver near-optimal decoding accuracy with small list sizes, paving the way for low-latency quantum error correction implementations.

title: GPU-accelerated semidefinite programming for causal games
summary: The process matrix formalism describes quantum correlations in scenarios without a fixed causal order between local laboratories. Operational signatures of such correlations can be investigated through causal games. A paradigmatic example is the Guess-Your-Neighbour's-Input game, in which two parties attempt to guess each other's inputs. Correlations compatible with any definite, or probabilistically mixed, causal order cannot achieve a winning probability exceeding $1/2$. The best process-matrix strategy currently known attains a value of approximately $0.6218$ using local dimension $d=5$, while the strongest known dimension-independent upper bound is $0.7592$. In this work, we investigate whether increasing the local dimension beyond $d = 5$ can narrow this gap. To this end, we employ a see-saw optimization scheme in which each step is formulated as a semidefinite program. For scalability, we develop a custom implementation of the SCS solver in which the dominant computational cost, the projection onto the positive-semidefinite cone, is offloaded to a GPU, yielding a six-fold speedup. Using this implementation, we explore local dimensions up to $d = 8$, and we do not find significant improvements over the value at $d=5$. Our results suggest that either qualitatively different strategies are required to approach the known upper bound, or that the bound itself is not tight.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether increasing local dimension beyond d=5 can improve the winning probability in the Guess-Your-Neighbour's-Input game under indefinite causal order, using a GPU-accelerated see-saw optimization scheme. The authors find no significant improvement up to d=8, suggesting the value at d=5 is near-optimal or the known upper bound is not tight.
AI.motivation: To determine whether increasing local Hilbert space dimension can narrow the gap between the best known process-matrix strategy (≈0.6218 at d=5) and the theoretical upper bound (≈0.7592) for the Guess-Your-Neighbour's-Input causal game.
AI.method: A see-saw optimization scheme with each step formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP), implemented with a custom GPU-accelerated SCS solver that offloads positive-semidefinite cone projection to achieve a six-fold speedup. Local dimensions up to d=8 are explored.
AI.result: No significant improvement in winning probability was observed beyond d=5 for local dimensions up to d=8.
AI.conclusion: Either qualitatively different strategies are needed to approach the known upper bound, or the bound itself is not tight.

title: Near-Optimal Learning of Local Lindbladians
summary: We study the problem of learning local Lindbladians from black-box access to the physical evolution, and the goal is to estimate all Hamiltonian and dissipative coefficients. We give an algorithm built directly from finite-time channel probes, which runs the unknown evolution for short times, estimates the corresponding Pauli transfer matrices from classical shadows, and converts these estimates into Lindbladian coefficients by stable local Fourier inversions. For fixed locality and bounded dissipative site degree, the uses of the dynamical evolution and total evolution time scale as $\widetilde{O}(Λ^2/\varepsilon^2)$ and $\widetilde{O}(Λ/\varepsilon^2)$ respectively, in the local dynamical strength bound $Λ$ and target accuracy $\varepsilon$, with only logarithmic dependence on the number of qubits. The algorithm is non-adaptive, uses no ancillas, and uses only random product states as inputs followed by random Pauli measurements. The method does not require knowing the support of the Lindbladian in advance. We complement the algorithm with matching lower bounds, showing that the learning algorithm is near-optimal both in physical dynamics accesses and in total evolution time. We construct a single-qubit dephasing Lindbladian family that already requires $Ω(Λ^2/\varepsilon^2)$ channel uses and $Ω(Λ/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, even for adaptive algorithms with arbitrary ancillas and measurements. In particular, the lower bounds imply that the Heisenberg-limited scaling achievable for Hamiltonian learning is information-theoretically impossible once dissipative coefficients must be estimated.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a learning algorithm for estimating Lindbladian coefficients (both Hamiltonian and dissipative) from black-box access to quantum evolution, achieving near-optimal sample and time complexity with logarithmic qubit dependence, along with matching lower bounds showing Heisenberg-limited scaling is impossible for dissipative learning.
AI.motivation: To solve the problem of learning local Lindbladians (characterizing both coherent Hamiltonian and incoherent dissipative dynamics) from black-box access to the physical evolution, with the goal of estimating all Hamiltonian and dissipative coefficients efficiently.
AI.method: The algorithm uses finite-time channel probes by running the unknown evolution for short times, estimates Pauli transfer matrices from classical shadows using random product states and random Pauli measurements, then converts these estimates into Lindbladian coefficients via stable local Fourier inversions. It is non-adaptive, uses no ancillas, and does not require prior knowledge of the Lindbladian's support.
AI.result: For fixed locality and bounded dissipative site degree, the dynamical evolution uses scale as $\widetilde{O}(Λ^2/\varepsilon^2)$ and total evolution time scales as $\widetilde{O}(Λ/\varepsilon^2)$, where Λ is the local dynamical strength bound and ε is target accuracy, with only logarithmic dependence on the number of qubits. Matching lower bounds show Ω(Λ^2/ε^2) channel uses and Ω(Λ/ε^2) total evolution time are necessary, even for adaptive algorithms with ancillas.
AI.conclusion: The learning algorithm is near-optimal both in physical dynamics accesses and total evolution time. The lower bounds imply that Heisenberg-limited scaling achievable for Hamiltonian learning is information-theoretically impossible once dissipative coefficients must be estimated.

title: Topological Codes Based on Space Groups
summary: Topological codes form one of the most important classes of stabilizer codes. Most existing algebraic constructions and analyses of topological codes assume translation invariance. Here we show that topological codes can arise in more general settings by incorporating point group operations. The central construction is a class of Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes called space-group codes, whose check operators are built from group-algebra templates over space groups that combine translations with point-group operations. We develop methods for analyzing topological properties of space-group codes using ring-modules and their invariant theory. At first glance, space-group codes might appear to complicate practical implementation; however, we find that they can exhibit greater locality than previous codes based purely on translations. Our framework thus extends the landscape of topological codes and opens up a broader design space for the co-design of topological codes with quantum computing platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces space-group codes, a new class of CSS topological codes that incorporate point-group operations (like rotations and reflections) beyond just translations, and develops algebraic methods to analyze their topological properties, showing they can achieve better locality than purely translation-based codes.
AI.motivation: Existing topological codes are almost exclusively built on translation invariance, limiting the design space. The authors aim to extend topological codes to more general settings by incorporating point-group symmetries (space groups) to broaden the landscape and enable co-design with quantum computing platforms.
AI.method: The authors construct a class of CSS codes called space-group codes, where check operators are built from group-algebra templates over space groups (combining translations with point-group operations). They develop analytical tools using ring-modules and invariant theory to study topological properties.
AI.result: Space-group codes can exhibit greater locality than previous codes based purely on translations, despite potentially appearing to complicate implementation.
AI.conclusion: The framework extends the landscape of topological codes and opens up a broader design space for co-designing topological codes with quantum computing platforms.

title: Benchmark of quantum algorithms for ground state preparation in the presence of noise
summary:
We compare the performance of representative cooling, adiabatic, and optimization algorithms for ground-state preparation in the presence of noise. Using an exactly solvable family of quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians subject to depolarizing noise, we derive the scaling of the achievable relative energy as a function of the noise rate and support these results with numerical simulations. The Hamiltonian exhibits two phases, separated by a quantum phase transition. As expected, the performance of the different algorithms depends on the phase: adiabatic evolution is favorable in the trivial phase, while a multi-frequency cooling algorithm, as proposed in [1], becomes competitive or superior in the topological phase, where gap-closing limits adiabatic protocols. We further present numerical results for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm [2], showing that it performs competitively with cooling in the trivial phase but is typically outperformed in the topological regime. Finally, we show that for this model the cooling protocol exhibits enhanced robustness to parameter imperfections, highlighting its potential advantage for realistic implementations of noisy quantum state preparation.
  The analytical approach developed here, in conjunction with numerical validation, establishes an extendable approach to benchmarking ground-state preparation algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks cooling, adiabatic, and optimization algorithms for ground-state preparation under noise, using solvable quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians. It finds that adiabatic evolution excels in the trivial phase, while multi-frequency cooling outperforms in the topological phase; QAOA is competitive in the trivial phase but not the topological one. Cooling also shows enhanced robustness to parameter imperfections.
AI.motivation: To systematically compare the performance of representative ground-state preparation algorithms (cooling, adiabatic, optimization) under realistic noise, and identify which regimes each algorithm is most suitable for.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of relative energy scaling under depolarizing noise for exactly solvable quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians, supported by numerical simulations. The Hamiltonian features two phases (trivial and topological) separated by a quantum phase transition.
AI.result: Adiabatic evolution performs best in the trivial phase; multi-frequency cooling is competitive/superior in the topological phase where gap-closing hinders adiabatic protocols. QAOA competes with cooling in the trivial phase but is typically outperformed in the topological regime. Cooling exhibits enhanced robustness to parameter imperfections.
AI.conclusion: The analytical approach combined with numerical validation provides an extendable benchmarking framework for ground-state preparation algorithms, and the results highlight the practical advantages of cooling protocols for noisy quantum state preparation.
